3.1.2 Exceptions 
Project operations as defined by Section 3.1.1 of this Offer of Settlement may be 
curtailed or suspended if required by operating emergency or as directed by the NYSCC. In 
addition, Project Operations as defined in Section 3.1.1 may be curtailed or suspended upon 
prior mutual agreement between the Licensee and the NYSDEC. In the event of any operating 
emergency beyond the control of the Licensee, the Project Operations as defined in Section 
3.1.1 may be curtailed or suspended for the time period necessary to rectify such condition. The 
Licensee shall notify the NYSDEC by phone call or email as soon as possible, but no later than 
five (5) business days after any such operating emergency or receipt of direction from the 
NYSCC. The Licensee shall notify the Commission consistent with requirements established 
by the Commission. 
3.1.3 Justification 
The Parties understand that the Project is located adjacent to NYSCC’s Lock C-3, which 
supports navigation associated with the Hudson River (Champlain Canal). Due to the railroad 
bridge located approximately 0.55 mile upstream of Lock C-3, the NYSCC routinely directs 
the Licensee to adjust the impoundment elevation to accommodate the safe passage of vessels 
through the Project’s impoundment as to provide adequate mast/vessel clearance under the 
bridge. In addition, NYSCC directs the Licensee to raise the impoundment to allow for deeper 
draft vessels to pass through the impoundment. In addition to navigation, in support of the larger 
Champlain Canal system, NYSCC directs impoundment level adjustments to support 
maintenance, inspections, emergencies, and construction activities of the NYSCC. Based on 
the studies and consultation performed in support of the relicensing, the Parties understand and 
agree that adjustments to the impoundment elevation are necessary in support of the NYSCC 
activities. Based on this understanding, the Parties have worked to define and differentiate 
Project operations for both the navigation season and the non-navigation season and believe 
that the agreements presented in Section 3.1.1 of this Offer of Settlement provide the best 
approach for addressing the navigational, hydropower, and aquatic resources associated with 
the Project.

Exhibit __ (CCE-31) - Part C

The Parties also understand that based on years of historic joint operations of the Project 
and Lock C-3 in support of navigation, changes in impoundment elevations at a rate of 26 inches 
per hour in the downward direction and 6 inches per hour in the upward direction provide a 
balance between navigation and the aquatic resources associated with the Project. In particular, 
these rates of change provide the responsiveness needed by the NYSCC to coordinate the in-
sequence lockages that are required to coordinate the passage of boat traffic through the 
Champlain Canal (i.e., vessels moving both upstream [north bound] and downstream [south 
bound] through Locks C-2, C-3, and C-4). In addition, these rates of changes ensure that the 
Project provides the desired continuous minimum year-round flows downstream of the Project 
during refill.  
3.2 
Bypass Flow 
3.2.1 General Agreements 
Within 1 month of the issuance and acceptance of the new license, or the Effective Date 
of the new license, whichever is later, and on an annual basis from April 1 to November 30, the 
Licensee shall provide a minimum release of 45 cubic feet per second (cfs) or inflow to the 
Project, whichever is less, to the Project’s bypassed reach. The bypass flow will be provided 
through flow over the Project’s spillway, flow through the Project’s intake bypass sluice gate, 
flow through the downstream fishway, when applicable, as defined in Section 3.3.1.3 of this 
Offer of Settlement, and/or by other means as determined by the Licensee. 
3.2.2 Exceptions 
Bypass flow as defined by Section 3.2.1 of this Offer of Settlement may be curtailed or 
suspended if required by operating emergency or as directed by the NYSCC. In addition, bypass 
flow as defined in Section 3.2.1 may be curtailed or suspended upon prior mutual agreement 
between the Licensee and the NYSDEC and the USFWS. In the event of any operating 
emergency beyond the control of the Licensee, Project Operations as defined in Section 3.2.1 
may be curtailed or suspended for the time period necessary to rectify such condition. The 
Licensee shall notify the NYSDEC and the USFWS by phone call or email as soon as possible, 
but no later than five (5) business days after any such operating emergency or receipt of

direction from the NYSCC. The Licensee shall notify the Commission consistent with

3.2.3 Justification 
Based on the studies performed in support of the relicensing process, the Parties agree 
that on a seasonal basis, there is a benefit of providing a continuous flow of water to the area 
immediately downstream of the Project’s spillway. As compared to keeping this area inundated, 
the Parties agree that maintaining a continuous flow through this immediate downstream area 
will benefit aquatic species that may attempt to use the area for spawning or nesting habitat. 
This Offer of Settlement does not require the Licensee to monitor or test the 
effectiveness of the bypass flow on any species, aquatic habitat, or water quality.  
3.3 
Fish Passage and Protection 
3.3.1 General Agreements 
3.3.1.1 Seasonal Upstream American Eel Ladder 
By the 2023 upstream migration season for American eel, on a seasonal basis, the 
Licensee will install a single ladder for the upstream movement of American eel in the Project’s 
tailrace (river right, looking downstream). The seasonal eel ladder will be installed and operated 
by April 1 of each year, and will be removed or closed on or after November 30 of each year. 
The installation, removal and/or closure of the seasonal ladder will be performed when river 
flows and conditions allow for the safe execution of such activities. If river flows or safety 
conditions prevent the installation and operation of the seasonal ladder by April 1st, or require 
the removal or closure of the ladder prior to November 30th, the Licensee will notify the 
NYSDEC and the USFWS within five (5) business days, and such information will be 
documented in the Fishway Operation and Maintenance Report (FOMR) as defined in Section 
3.3.3 of this Offer of Settlement. 
The design of the seasonal upstream eel ladder will be based on the conceptual design 
presented in Attachment C to this Offer of Settlement and will be further designed and

3.3.1.2 Seasonal Upstream Fish Passage 
Within one year following the installation of upstream passage facilities at the 
downstream Mechanicville Project (FERC Project No. 6032), passage for the upstream

be designed in consultation with, and through approval by, the USFWS and the NYSDEC. In 
support of meeting the agreed-upon schedule, the USFWS and the NYSDEC will notify 
NYSEG four years prior to the required date for installing the upstream fishway at the Upper 
Mechanicville Project. If it is not possible to provide at least 4 years’ advance notification, the 
installation date at Upper Mechanicville may be delayed upon agreement among the Licensee, 
the USFWS, and the NYSDEC.

structure to ensure compliance with the USFWS Criteria, including compliance with 
performance standards for water velocities, attraction flows, plunge pool depths, and all other

maintenance activities needed to facilitate safe and effective passage (e.g., debris removal from 
the sluice gate and/or plunge pool). In addition, the Licensee may curtail or suspend fish 
protection and passage measures upon prior mutual agreement between the Licensee, the 
USFWS, and the NYSDEC. In the event of any operating emergency beyond the control of the 
Licensee, the Licensee may curtail or suspend fish protection and passage measures for the time 
period necessary to rectify such an operating emergency. The Licensee shall notify the 
NYSDEC and the USFWS as soon as possible by phone or email, but no later than five (5) 
business days after any such operating emergency. Any curtailment or suspension of fish 
passage activities will be documented in the FOMR as defined in Section 3.3.3 of this Offer of 
Settlement. The Licensee shall notify the Commission consistent with requirements established 
by the Commission. 
3.3.6 Justification 
The lock structures associated with each of the downstream projects are providing a 
means for some fish to migrate to the Upper Mechanicville Project. In addition, the downstream 
Green Island Project (FERC Project No. 13), is under a Commission Compliance Order to 
complete upstream passage facilities (an eel ladders and fish lifts) by the end of 2021. The 
Parties agree that Lock C-3, located adjacent to the Project, is also providing the means for 
some fish to migrate upstream of the Project. Therefore, the existing river-wide system is 
providing an opportunity for some fish to migrate upstream of the Project. However, the Parties 
also agree that over the proposed 50-year term of the Project’s new license, upstream migration 
Page 24 of 46
Exhibit __ (CCE-31) - Part C 


--- Page 1184 ---
4846-7610-7699.3 
 
Upper Mechanicville Hydroelectric Project 
Offer of Settlement 
 
 
22 
 
may be improved. Therefore, given the presence of Lock C-3 on river left, the Parties believe 
that the installation of a seasonal ladder to promote the upstream migration of American eel on 
river right would be beneficial to the species. This location is consistent with the surveys 
performed in support of the relicensing and thus the Parties agree to the installation of a seasonal 
eel ladder in the Project’s tailrace.  
Regarding upstream passage for other seasonal upstream migrating species, the Parties 
agree that following the installation of potential upstream passage at the downstream 
Mechanicville Project, additional upstream passage at the Upper Mechanicville Project may be 
required. Therefore, the Parties agree that within one year of upstream fish passage being 
installed at the Mechanicville Project, similar upstream passage will be installed at the Upper 
Mechanicville Project. 
Regarding downstream fish passage and protection, the Parties agree that the Project’s 
two large, slow-moving turbines, in combination with the Project’s lower head design, provide 
a more fish-friendly option for many of the fish that pass through the Project’s intake and 
turbines than other sites in the watershed. Due to this unique design feature, the Parties agree 
that the Project is considered less detrimental to many of the fish species associated with the 
Hudson River and the Project area than other sites in the watershed. However, due to a lack of 
Project-specific data, in combination with the NYSDEC’s goal of 98% survivability of 
American eels passing downstream of the Project, the Parties have concluded that American 
eels must be excluded from the Project’s intake and passed downstream using measures 
consistent with the USFWS’ Fish Passage Engineering Design Criteria.

Stream Flow and Water Level Monitoring Plan 
3.4.1 General Agreements 
The Licensee shall develop and maintain a Stream Flow and Water Level Monitoring 
Plan (Monitoring Plan) in consultation with and approved by the NYSDEC and the USFWS. 
The approved Monitoring Plan and the identification of all equipment (e.g., gauges, markers, 
and/or other measuring devices) to determine head pond elevation, bypass flow, and rate of 
impoundment elevation change will be filed with the Commission within 6 months of the

issuance and acceptance of the new license, or the Effective Date of the new license, whichever 
is later,. The Monitoring Plan and the associated equipment will provide a means of independent 
verification by the NYSDEC and the USFWS of the Project’s minimum bypass flow. The 
Licensee shall ensure that all monitoring equipment required by the Monitoring Plan, including 
head pond and/or tail water gauges, shall be made operational and calibrated within 18 months

3.4.2 Record Keeping 
As to be defined by the Stream Flow and Water Level Monitoring Plan, the Licensee 
shall keep accurate and sufficient records of the impoundment elevations, bypass flows, and the 
rate of impoundment elevation change. Such data shall be maintained in spreadsheet format in 
intervals ranging from 15 minutes to 1 hour, and in increments ranging from 0.1 foot to 1.0 
foot. A copy of the Monitoring Plan and all associated records will be made available for visual 
inspection at the Licensee’s Hydro Site within 5 business days of a request from the NYSDEC, 
or provided to the NYSDEC in written form within 30 days of the Licensee’s receipt of a written 
request for such records by the NYSDEC. In support of implementing the Monitoring Plan, the 
NYSDEC will provide the Licensee with a contact person to receive such information. In 
addition, the Licensee will provide to the NYSDEC the name of a 7 day-per-week contact 
person or persons to provide timely verification of monitored flows, rate of impoundment 
elevation change, and responses to questions regarding abnormal or emergency conditions. 
3.4.3 Justification 
The Parties believe that the development of a Stream Flow and Water Level Monitoring 
Plan and the associated measurement and data management activities are an essential 
component of a water flow and elevation management program. Such a Monitoring Plan, and 
the associated implementation of the Plan, provides the tools necessary to verify the water flows 
and elevations agreed to in this Offer of Settlement, and provides a systematic means of tracking 
flow and elevation compliance. Aside from providing the agencies a means to independently 
monitor bypass flows, the visual gauge(s) or marker(s) will be useful to the Licensee as well.

The purpose of the Monitoring Plan is to allow the NYSDEC and the USFWS an 
independent means to determine how closely the Project complies with required operations. 
While the Licensee will be allowed to fluctuate the impoundment as directed by the NYSCC in 
support of navigation and canal operations, the Parties believe that the ability to monitor the 
required bypass flow and rate of impoundment elevation change is essential to the Project’s 
compliance program. Through the establishment of a means (gauge[s] and/or marker[s]) to 
verify the Project’s bypass flow, as well as record keeping to verify the rate of impoundment 
elevation change, the Parties will have a sufficient means of confirming the Project’s 
compliance with the agreed-to operational measures. 
3.5 
Threatened and Endangered Species 
3.5.1 General Agreements 
The Licensee has consulted with the USFWS and the NYSDEC and has identified the 
northern long-eared bat and bald eagle as species of concern that could be found within the 
Project area. In order to address the management of these species relative to Project operations, 
the Licensee has developed a Northern Long-Eared Bat Management Plan and Bald Eagle 
Management Plan in consultation with, and with the approval of, the NYSDEC and the 
USFWS. Copies of the approved plans are presented in Attachments A and B, respectively, to 
this Offer of Settlement. The plans include measures to provide protection to both northern 
long-eared bats and bald eagles. Upon issuance of the new license by the Commission, the 
Licensee will implement the Northern Long-Eared Bat Management and Bald Eagle 
Management Plans. 
3.5.2 Justification 
The northern long-eared bat is protected under the Endangered Species Act and the bald 
eagle is protected under the Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act and the Migratory Bird 
Treaty Act. Additionally, both species are protected by the State of New York. Removal of trees 
could potentially affect northern long-eared bats and bald eagles. The Parties agree that 
implementation of the Northern Long-Eared Bat and Bald Eagle Management Plans, presented

in Attachments A and B, respectively, to this Offer of Settlement will minimize future Project-
related impacts that may affect these species. 
3.6 
Invasive Species 
3.6.1 General Agreements 
Upon the issuance and acceptance of the new license, or the Effective Date of the new 
license, whichever is later, the Licensee will implement the Invasive Species Management Plan 
that has been developed in consultation with the NYSDEC and the USFWS. A copy of the 
approved plan is presented in Attachment D to this Offer of Settlement. The plan includes 
measures to prevent or limit the introduction and/or spread of invasive species during 
construction, maintenance, and operational activities associated with the Project, as defined by 
the NYSDEC Office of Invasive Species Coordination. 
3.6.2 Justification 
Although no invasive species were identified within the Project boundary during the 
relicensing studies, the Parties agree that implementation of the Invasive Species Management 
Plan presented in Attachment D to this Offer of Settlement will be beneficial to help prevent 
the introduction of invasive species to the Project through construction activities or hydropower 
operations.

Northern Long-Eared Bat Management Plan 
 
 
In consultation with the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (NYSDEC) 
and the United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS), New York State Electric & Gas 
Corporation (NYSEG or the Licensee) has developed this management plan in support of 
managing northern long-eared bats associated with NYSEG’s Upper Mechanicville Hydroelectric 
Project throughout the term of the new license to be issued by the Federal Energy Regulatory 
Commission (FERC). 
Management Activities 
To date, no northern long-eared bats or occupied maternity roost trees or hibernacula have been 
identified within the Project boundary or areas immediately adjacent to the Project boundary. If 
through the routine maintenance activities an occupied maternity roost tree or hibernacula are 
discovered within the Project boundary, the Licensee will notify the NYSDEC and the USFWS 
within 72 hours of any such discovery. 
Prior to any tree clearing within the Project boundary or areas immediately adjacent to the Project 
boundary, the Licensee will observe the area to be cleared for occupied maternity roost trees, 
roosting trees, sloughing bark, or dead limbs that can provide northern long-eared bat habitat. If 
such occupied trees, occupied bark, or occupied limbs are discovered, the NYSDEC and the 
USFWS will be consulted prior to tree-clearing activities. In addition, the Licensee shall follow 
the following tree clearing guidelines, as applicable. 
1. The Licensee may remove hazard trees that the Licensee has a reasonable basis to believe 
pose a material threat to human life or property at any time without prior consultation with 
the NYSDEC and the USFWS and inform the NYSDEC and the USFWS if any bats are 
observed. 
Page 30 of 46
Exhibit __ (CCE-31) - Part C 


--- Page 1190 ---
4846-7610-7699.3 
 
 
 
Attachment A-2 
 
2. The Licensee may remove any trees <3 inches diameter at breast height (dbh) at any time 
without prior consultation with, or notification to, the NYSDEC and the USFWS so long 
as their removal will not damage any adjacent trees that are larger in size. 
3. The Licensee may remove suitable roost trees ≥3 inches dbh between October 1 and March 
31 without prior consultation with, or notification to, the NYSDEC and the USFWS.  
4. Should the Licensee find it necessary to remove or be required by FERC to remove suitable 
roost trees ≥3 inches dbh between April 1 and September 30, the Licensee will consult with 
the USFWS pursuant to the Endangered Species Act. The Licensee will also consult with 
the NYSDEC and may request a determination under NYCRR Part 182.9 as to whether a 
proposed activity is likely to result in the take or taking of listed bat species and/or may 
apply for an incidental take permit in accordance with NYCRR Part 182.11. 
It is not the intent of this plan to hold the Licensee to a higher standard than the applicable laws 
surrounding the species. Accordingly, this plan shall be subject to change to be consistent with any 
changes in applicable law or with any change in the Endangered or Threatened listing status of the 
species that would cause the tree clearing guidelines identified above to be modified consistent 
with applicable regulations and industry best practices.

Bald Eagle Management Plan 
 
 
In consultation with the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (NYSDEC) 
and the United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS), New York State Electric & Gas 
Corporation (NYSEG or the Licensee) has developed this management plan in support of 
managing bald eagles (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) associated with NYSEG’s Upper Mechanicville 
Hydroelectric Project throughout the term of the new license to be issued by the Federal Energy 
Regulatory Commission (FERC). 
Management Activities 
A bald eagle nest is located on the eastern shore of the Hudson River approximately 2,400 feet 
downstream of the Upper Mechanicville Dam outside of the Project boundary; therefore, a bald 
eagle could potentially occur within the Project impact area. 
Prior to any tree clearing within the Project boundary or areas immediately adjacent to the Project 
boundary, the area to be cleared will be observed for bald eagle nests by the Licensee. If such nests 
are discovered, the NYSDEC and the USFWS will be consulted prior to tree-clearing activities 
and the tree-clearing activities will be performed in accordance with the applicable regulations and 
guidance. 
During the nesting season (January 1 through September 30), no tree clearing will occur within 
330 feet of, and no construction activities will occur within 660 feet of, any known bald eagle nests 
by the Licensee or its contractors. The Licensee will consult with the NYSDEC and the USFWS 
regarding tree clearing or construction activities that cannot meet these conditions.

Attachment D-1 
 
Upper Mechanicville Hydroelectric Project 
(FERC No. 2934) 
 
Invasive Plant Species Management Plan 
 
 
In consultation with the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (NYSDEC) 
and the United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS), New York State Electric & Gas 
Corporation (NYSEG or the Licensee) has developed this management plan in support of 
managing invasive species associated with NYSEG’s Upper Mechanicville Hydroelectric Project 
throughout the term of the new license to be issued by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission 
(FERC). 
Activities Associated with Routine Maintenance 
The following activities will be performed by NYSEG in order to assist in preventing the 
establishment and/or spreading of invasive plant species: 
 The Licensee will continue to maintain Project grounds located within the Project’s FERC 
Project boundary in a manner that helps prevent the introduction and spread of invasive species 
within the Project’s established FERC Project boundary. 
 The Licensee will not actively plant any terrestrial plants listed as Prohibited or Regulated 
pursuant to 6 NYCRR Part 575 by the NYSDEC. 
 When in-water work is required, the Licensee and/or contracted personnel will comply with 
the NYSDEC-recommended measures (clean, drain, and dry) for preventing the introduction 
and/or spread of aquatic invasive plant species. 
 The Licensee will monitor areas of disturbance caused by routine operation or maintenance 
activities within the Project boundary to ensure that invasive species do not out-compete 
desirable vegetation during the reestablishment phase. 
 The Licensee will instruct all work personnel to visually inspect all exposed boating equipment 
used for maintenance activities for attached invasive species. 
 The Licensee will clean and dry boats and trailers used for maintenance activities that come in 
contact with the water. 
Page 40 of 46
Exhibit __ (CCE-31) - Part C 


--- Page 1200 ---
4846-7610-7699.3 
 
 
 
Attachment D-2 
 
 The Licensee will remove any visible plants or animals before entering the water or leaving 
the site. Plants and animals are to be discarded in an upland area. 
Activities Associated with Construction or Major Maintenance 
Prior to any construction or major maintenance activities that require consultation with the 
NYSDEC, the Licensee will consult with the NYSDEC regarding the best management practices 
to be employed to help prevent the introduction and/or spread of invasive species within the area 
associated with the activity to be performed. 
In addition to activity-specific best management practices that may be developed through 
consultation with the NYSDEC, the Licensee will employ the following best management 
practices during construction and major maintenance activities.  
 Clean and dry boats and trailers used for construction or major maintenance activities that 
come in contact with the water. 
 Remove visible plants or animals before entering the water or leaving the site. Plants and 
animals are to be discarded in an upland area. 
During construction 
 Workers will be trained to identify invasive plants and informed of the importance of 
infestation prevention. 
 Obvious vegetative material will be removed from construction equipment before allowing the 
equipment to enter an invasive-free area. 
 Invasive plants that could potentially be spread by construction equipment or workers will be 
removed. Along access roads, invasive plants will be identified and controlled to avoid 
introducing them into invasive-free areas. 
 Where practical, gravel and fill will come from invasive-free sources to avoid introducing 
invasive vegetation to the construction site. 
 Where practical, certified invasive-free straw, mulch, fiber rolls, and sediment logs will be 
used for erosion and sediment control.

Exhibit __ (CCE-31) - Part C

4846-7610-7699.3 
 
 
 
Attachment D-3 
 
During seeding and planting 
 Where practical, soil amendments (if any) and mulches will be obtained from invasive-free 
sources. 
 The Licensee will make a reasonable effort to use only native seed mixes for reseeding 
disturbed areas (as provided by the NYSDEC, such native seed and seed mixes include Big 
Bluestem (Andropogon gerardii), Little Bluestem (Schizachyrium scoparium), Bottlebrush 
Grass (Elymus hystrix), Indiangrass (Sorghastrum nutans), Canada Wildrye (Elymus 
canadensis), Deertongue (Dicanthelium clandestinum) and Switchgrass (Pallicum virgatum)). 
Species examples are from Vegetating with Native Grasses in Northeastern North America 
(USDA-NRCS and Duck Unlimited Canada). 
 Seeding and planting operations and maintenance will be conducted in a manner to ensure 
vigorous growth of desirable vegetation and discourage invasive species. 
 Bare ground will be seeded as quickly as possible following disturbance. 
 Seeded sites will be monitored for infestation by invasive species. 
 Identified invasive plant species at monitored sites will be treated in the first full growing 
season.  
 Where practical, mulch will be used to limit the amount of unwanted seed sources reaching 
bare soil.  
 The Licensee will ensure that all construction contractors under its control are aware of, and 
comply with, the terms listed above. 
Post construction 
 The Licensee will monitor any areas of disturbance caused by construction activities on lands 
owned by the Licensee within the Project boundary as needed to ensure that invasive species 
have not out-competed desirable vegetation during the reestablishment.

INTRODUCTION 
1. 
On April 1, 2019, New York State Electric & Gas Corporation (NYSEG) filed, 
pursuant to sections 4(e) and 15 of the Federal Power Act (FPA),1 an application for a 
new license to continue operation and maintenance of the Upper Mechanicville 
Hydroelectric Project No. 2934 (Upper Mechanicville Project or project).  The 
16.53-megawatt (MW) project is located on the Hudson River in Saratoga and Rensselaer 
Counties, New York.2  The project does not occupy federal land.   
2. 
As discussed below, this order issues a new license for the project. 
BACKGROUND 
3. 
The Commission issued the original license for the project on April 23, 1981, with 
an effective date of April 1, 1981, and an expiration date of March 31, 2021.3   
4. 
On May 28, 2019, the Commission issued a public notice that was published in the 
Federal Register accepting the application for filing and setting July 29, 2019, as the 
deadline for filing motions to intervene and protests.4  The U.S. Department of the 
Interior (Interior) and New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (New

PROJECT DESCRIPTION 
A. 
Project Area 
12. 
The Hudson River originates in the Adirondack Mountains and flows south 315 
river miles to New York Harbor, where the river meets the Atlantic Ocean.  The Hudson 
River watershed encompasses approximately 13,400 square miles and lies almost entirely 
(93%) within the state of New York.  The Upper Mechanicville Project is located at river 
mile 167 on the Hudson River in Saratoga and Rensselaer Counties, New York.    
13. 
The Champlain Canal, which is part of the New York State Canal System, begins 
at river mile 158 on the Hudson River near Waterford, New York.  The canal is confluent 
with the river for 37 miles upstream to Fort Edward, New York, where the it branches off 
towards Lake Champlain as an artificial channel that is separate from, and no longer 
confluent with, the Hudson River.  The Champlain Canal has 11 navigation locks that 
provide passage for recreational and commercial vessels between the Hudson River and 
Lake Champlain.   
14. 
The project is located on the portion of the Champlain Canal that is confluent with 
the Hudson River.  There are six lock and dams on this portion of the Champlain Canal 
that are operated by the Canal Corporation to support navigation.  Four of these lock and 
dams have existing FERC-licensed or exempted hydroelectric projects, including, from 
upstream to downstream:  Fort Miller Project No. 4226 at Lock C6, Stillwater Project No. 
4684 at Lock C4, Upper Mechanicville Project at Lock C3, and Mechanicville Project 
No. 6032 at Lock C2.9  The Green Island Project No. 13 is located in Troy, New York, 
about 5 river miles downstream of Lock C1, at a lock and dam that is operated by the 
U.S. Army Corps of Engineers for navigation purposes and is the lowermost dam on the 
mainstem Hudson River.    
                                                          
9 The lock and dams on the Champlain Canal are numbered consecutively, starting 
with the most downstream lock and dam (Lock C1) at Waterford, New York and 
increasing in number moving upstream (towards Lake Champlain).

B. 
Project Facilities 
15. 
The Upper Mechanicville Project includes a 700-foot-long concrete gravity dam 
that has three spillway bays, each of which extends 222 feet across the length of the dam 
and is separated by 7.5-foot to 10.5-foot-wide concrete piers.  Each spillway bay has a 
crest elevation of 66.6 feet10 and contains a 222-foot-wide by 6-foot-high pneumatically 
operated Obermeyer crest gate.   
16. 
The project impoundment is 1.8 miles long and has a surface area of 380 acres and 
a gross storage capacity of 10,735 acre-feet at a normal pool elevation of 72.6 feet (top of 
the fully raised crest gates).  An earthen embankment is located on the east side of the 
river (opposite the powerhouse) that serves to retain water to help maintain the project 
impoundment.   
17. 
The intake channel leading to the powerhouse has three guide walls:  two 
reinforced-concrete guide walls and one guide wall consisting of three 35-foot-diameter 
cellular cofferdam walls constructed of sheet piling.  An intake bypass sluice gate (sluice 
gate, hereafter) is located on the east guide wall of the intake channel immediately 
upstream of the project’s intake.  The sluice gate is 20 feet wide and 16.5 feet deep at the 
gate sill and has a 7.5-foot-high gate that is used to pass ice and debris downstream of the 
dam. 
18. 
The 105.5-foot by 122-foot powerhouse contains two 12,780-horsepower (or 
9,585-kilowatt [kW]) vertical Kaplan turbines and two Siemens-Allis generators each 
having a rated capacity of 8,265 kW.  The trash racks covering the intakes have a clear 
spacing of 5.5 inches.  Water exiting the powerhouse flows into an excavated tailrace 
channel that is 1,200 feet long, 120 feet wide, and contains a bi-level bottom11 that is 
designed to minimize cross-currents to reduce the effects of the project on navigation.  
Two guide walls are present along the uppermost 330 feet (west side) and 120 feet (east 
side) of the tailrace channel.  A 275-foot-long bypassed reach is present downstream of 
the project dam.  
                                                          
10 All elevations in this order are referenced to the National Geodetic Vertical 
Datum of 1929 (NGVD 29).   
11 The bi-level bottom refers to the sloped bottom of the riverbed (3.5 feet higher 
on the east side) to guide flows exiting the powerhouse away from the navigation lock to 
help minimize cross-currents, which can negatively affect vessel maneuverability in the 
vicinity of Lock C3.

19. 
Project power is transmitted through a 1.10-mile-long, 34.5-kilovolt transmission

of Stillwater, New York.   
20. 
Under the current license, the upstream portion of Lock C3 of the Champlain 
Canal, including the upstream approach wall and upstream miter gates,12 are project 
facilities.   
21. 
There are no recreation facilities associated with the project.

A more detailed project description is contained in ordering paragraph (B)(2). 
C. 
Current Project Operation 
23. 
The project is operated in a run-of-river mode,13 as modified to support navigation 
on the Champlain Canal.14  NYSEG maintains the impoundment at a target elevation of 
72.6 feet.  However, the Canal Corporation routinely requests that NYSEG adjust the 
surface elevation of the impoundment to support navigation.  Such adjustments are most 
frequent during the navigation season, from mid-May through mid-October,15 when the 
impoundment is lowered (generally to an elevation of 70.8 feet or 69.1 feet, but on 
occasion to the dam crest itself, elevation of 66.6 feet) to allow vessels to pass underneath 
a low-clearance railroad bridge that spans the project impoundment 3,100 feet upstream 
of the project dam.  These impoundment drawdowns are made by spilling water over the 
project’s crest gates.  There are also times during the navigation season that the Canal 
Corportion requests that NYSEG raise the impoundment (achieved by reducing flow 
through the powerhouse) to facilitate the passage of deep draft vessels through the project 
impoundment.  Outside of the navigation season, from mid-October through mid-May, 
the Canal Corporation occasionally requests adjustments to the surface elevation of the 
impoundment to support maintenance activities at Lock C3.  Therefore, during both the

Project No. 2934-029

navigation season and to a lesser extent, the non-navigation season, there are times when 
the project is not operated in a run-of-river mode because when the impoundment is 
being lowered (e.g., to support vessel passage), outflow from the project exceeds inflow, 
and when the impoundment is being refilled or raised (e.g., following a navigation-
related impoundment drawdown), project outflow is less than inflow.   
24. 
During the water level adjustments described above, NYSEG ensures the rates of 
change in impoundment elevation do not exceed 26 inches per hour in the downward 
direction and 6 inches per hour in the upward direction.  These rates of change provide 
the responsiveness needed by the Canal Corporation to coordinate the in-sequence 
lockages that are necessary to facilitate the passage of vessel traffic through the 
Champlain Canal (i.e., boats moving both upstream and downstream through Locks C2, 
C3, and C4).    
25. 
When the project is operating, flows in excess of those needed to support 
navigation enter the intake channel, pass through the powerhouse, and are discharged  
into the tailrace.  During normal and low-flow conditions, the project is operated such 
that the pneumatic crest gates in two of the three spillway bays are in the fully raised 
position, with the top of the third crest gate set approximately 3 inches above the desired 
impoundment elevation.16  This allows the project to start spilling shortly after any station 
trips to ensure the continuity of downstream flow.   
26. 
If the available inflow is below the minimum hydraulic capacity of the project 
(1,200 cubic feet per second [cfs]), the turbines are taken offline and the crest gates are 
adjusted to maintain the impoundment at an elevation of 72.6 feet, or the elevation 
requested by the Canal Corporation for navigation purposes.  When inflows exceed the 
project’s maximum hydraulic capacity (12,000 cfs), the pneumatic crest gates are used to 
spill flows in excess of those needed to maintain the desired impoundment elevation.   
27. 
Impoundment elevations are maintained by the project’s microprocessor-based 
control system, which adjusts turbine flow as necessary to maintain the desired 
impoundment elevation.  The project is operated remotely from NYSEG’s Energy 
Control Center in Vestal, New York, but NYSEG staff typically visit the project two to 
three times per week.

Proposed Operation and Environmental Measures 
28. 
NYSEG’s proposed operation and environmental measures for relicensing the 
Upper Mechanicville Project, described in the license application, were modified by the

April 8, 2020 Settlement Agreement.  Proposed operations and the substantive proposed 
environmental measures are described below. 
29. 
To minimize potential shoreline erosion, NYSEG proposes to continue operating 
the project in a run-of-river mode and to maintain the impoundment at an elevation of at 
least 72.1 feet (no lower than 6 inches below the target impoundment elevation of 72.6 
feet, which corresponds to the top of the fully raised crest gates), unless directed 
otherwise by the Canal Corporation in support of navigation on the Champlain Canal 
(section 3.1 of the Settlement Agreement). 
30. 
To support navigation activity on the Champlain Canal and ensure the continuity 
of downstream flow (during impoundment refill), NYSEG proposes to continue limiting 
the rate of change in impoundment elevation to 26 inches per hour in the downward 
direction (when the impoundment is being lowered) and 6 inches per hour in the upward 
direction (when the impoundment is being raised or refilled), unless otherwise directed 
by the Canal Corporation (section 3.1 of the Settlement Agreement). 
31. 
To support downstream habitat and provide a continuous circulation of water in 
the bypassed reach, NYSEG proposes to release a seasonal minimum flow of 45 cfs, or 
project inflow, if less, into the bypassed reach from April 1 through November 30 of each 
year (section 3.2 of the Settlement Agreement).  
32. 
To verify compliance with the agreed-upon impoundment elevations, minimum 
flow, and rates of change in impoundment elevation, NYSEG proposes to develop a 
stream flow and water level monitoring plan in consultation with New York DEC and 
FWS (section 3.4 of the Settlement Agreement).   
33. 
To improve upstream passage opportunities for American eel, NYSEG proposes to 
install and operate an eel ladder in the project’s tailrace on a seasonal basis, from April 1 
through November 30, beginning with the 2023 migration season (section 3.3 of the 
Settlement Agreement).  
34. 
To protect and provide passage for eels migrating downstream, NYSEG proposes 
to install a downstream eel passage system by September 30, 2025, that consists of 
permanent trash racks with a 0.75-inch clear spacing and a non-turbine route of passage 
(downstream bypass) that would be operated on a seasonal basis from ice-out (typically 
mid- to late-March) through November 30 (section 3.3 of the Settlement Agreement). 
35. 
To support the upstream migration of fish species within the Hudson River, 
NYSEG proposes to install an upstream fishway within one year of the installation of 
upstream fish passage facilities at the downstream Mechanicville Project (section 3.3 of 
the Settlement Agreement).

E. 
Project Boundary 
42. 
The current project boundary encloses the impoundment (to a contour elevation of 
72.6 feet), dam, powerhouse, the upstream portion of Lock C3 (i.e., that portion upstream 
of the project dam), and the transmission line corridor.   
43. 
NYSEG proposes to expand the project boundary by 5.75 acres to include the 
excavated tailrace channel and its accompanying guide walls (containing the bi-level 
bottom feature described above) as well as the earthen embankment located on the east 
side of the river.

SUMMARY OF LICENSE REQUIREMENTS 
44. 
This license, which authorizes 16.53 MW of renewable energy generation 
capacity, requires the proposed measures listed above, the staff-recommended 
modifications and additional measures described below, the conditions required by New 
York DEC’s water quality certification (Appendix A), and the conditions required by 
FWS’s section 18 fishway prescription (Appendix B).  Combined, these measures will 
protect water quality, fisheries, terrestrial, and cultural resources at the project.   
45. 
To verify compliance with the project’s operational requirements, Article 403 
requires NYSEG to develop an operation compliance monitoring plan that incorporates 
the provisions of the proposed stream flow and water level monitoring plan and 
additional provisions necessary for compliance purposes, including procedures for the 
annual reporting of monitoring data to the Commission and filing the plan with the 
Commission for final approval.   
46. 
To protect cultural resources, Article 405 requires NYSEG to develop an HPMP  
pursuant to a Programmatic Agreement (PA) for the project that was executed on 
December 2, 2020.    
47. 
To ensure the project boundary encloses all lands, waters, works, and facilities 
necessary for operation and maintenance of the project, this license requires NYSEG to 
revise the project boundary to enclose the entire Lock C3 of the Champlain Canal. 
WATER QUALITY CERTIFICATION 
48. 
Under section 401(a)(1) of the Clean Water Act (CWA),18 the Commission may 
not issue a license authorizing the construction or operation of a hydroelectric project 
unless the state water quality certifying agency either has issued water quality 
certification (certification) for the project or has waived certification by failing to act on a 
request for certification within a reasonable period of time, not to exceed one year.  
Section 401(d) of the CWA provides that the certification shall become a condition of 
any federal license that authorizes construction or operation of the project.19 
49. 
On January 24, 2020, NYSEG applied to New York DEC for water quality 
certification for the Upper Mechanicville Project.  New York DEC received the 
application on January 27, 2020.  New York DEC issued a certification for the project on 
December 30, 2020.  The certification includes 36 conditions, 8 of which are discussed in 
the next paragraph.  The remaining 28 conditions are general or administrative in nature

COASTAL ZONE MANAGEMENT ACT 
52. 
Under section 307(c)(3)(A) of the Coastal Zone Management Act (CZMA),22 the 
Commission cannot issue a license for a project within or affecting a state’s coastal zone 
unless the state’s coastal zone management agency concurs with the license applicant’s 
certification of consistency with the state’s CZMA program, or the agency’s concurrence 
is conclusively presumed by its failure to act within 6 months of its receipt of the 
applicant’s certification.   
53. 
In an e-mail dated September 14, 2015, and filed with NYSEG’s license 
application, the New York State Department of State indicates that the Upper 
Mechanicville Project is not located within the State of New York’s coastal area and that 
it does not anticipate the need for a consistency review because project effects on the 
coastal area are unlikely.    
SECTION 18 FISHWAY PRESCRIPTIONS 
54. 
Section 18 of the FPA23 provides that the Commission shall require the 
construction, maintenance, and operation by a licensee of such fishways as may be 
prescribed by the Secretary of the Interior or the Secretary of Commerce, as appropriate. 
55. 
On January 27, 2020, Interior filed a preliminary fishway prescription.  On 
September 21, 2020, FWS filed, on Interior’s behalf, a modified section 18 fishway 
prescription.  The modified prescription requires NYSEG to:  
(1) Install an eel ladder at the project by the 2023 passage season (prescriptions 
9.3.1, 9.7.2);    
(2) Install a downstream eel passage system at the project by September 30, 2025, 
consisting of trash racks with a 0.75-inch clear spacing and downstream bypass 
structures (sluice gate and submerged low-level outlet), and provide a continuous 
downstream flow of at least 600 cfs during the downstream passage season  
(prescriptions 9.3.1, 9.4, and 9.7.1); 
(3) Design the required eel ladder and downstream eel passage system to handle any 
anticipated eel movements at the project (prescription 9.1); 
(4) Operate the required upstream and downstream fishways during the designated 
migration period—April 1 through November 30 for upstream passage and ice-

59. 
In the EA, staff identified one federally listed species that may occur in Saratoga 
and Rensselaer Counties, New York, and could be affected by relicensing the Upper 
Mechanicville Project; the threatened northern long-eared bat (Myotis septentrionalis).  
Staff concluded that relicensing the project with the proposed measures in NYSEG’s 
Northern Long-Eared Bat Management Plan (filed as Appendix A of the Settlement 
Agreement) may affect the northern long-eared bat, but any incidental take that may 
result from these activities is not prohibited under the final 4(d) rule26 for the northern 
long-eared bat.27  Commission staff also concluded that no designated or proposed 
critical habitat for this species occurs within the project boundary. 
60. 
In a letter filed January 27, 2020, Interior states that “[b]ased on the 
measures…included in [NYSEG’s Northern Long-eared Bat Management Plan], any take 
that may occur incidental to this project is not prohibited under the final 4(d) rule.  No 
further ESA coordination or consultation will be required if the [plan] is approved by the 
Service.”  In the same letter, Interior recommends implementation of NYSEG’s Northern 
Long-Eared Bat Management Plan filed with the Settlement Agreement.  Implementation 
of the Northern Long-Eared Bat Management Plan is required by certification condition 
11.  Therefore, no further action under the ESA is required. 
NATIONAL HISTORIC PRESERVATION ACT 
61. 
Under section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA)28 and its 
implementing regulations,29 federal agencies must consider the effect of any proposed 
undertaking on properties listed or eligible for listing in the National Register, defined as 
historic properties, and afford the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation a reasonable 
opportunity to comment on the undertaking.  This process generally requires the 
Commission to consult with the State Historic Preservation Office (SHPO) to determine 
whether and how a proposed action may affect historic properties, and to seek ways to 
avoid or minimize any adverse effects.

RECOMMENDATIONS OF FEDERAL AND STATE FISH AND WILDLIFE 
AGENCIES PURSUANT TO SECTION 10(j) OF THE FPA 
63. 
Section 10(j)(1) of the FPA31 requires the Commission, when issuing a license, to 
include conditions based on recommendations submitted by federal and state fish and 
wildlife agencies pursuant to the Fish and Wildlife Coordination Act,32 to “adequately 
and equitably protect, mitigate damages to, and enhance fish and wildlife (including 
related spawning grounds and habitat)” affected by the project. 
64. 
In response to the Commission’s November 29, 2019 notice that the project was 
ready for environmental analysis, Interior, on January 27, 2020, filed three fish and 
wildlife recommendations pursuant to section 10(j).  Subsequent to that filing, as noted 
above, NYSEG, FWS, and other parties executed the Settlement Agreement.  In its 
comments on the Settlement Agreement, filed April 21, 2020, Interior states that the 12 
measures in the Settlement Agreement (Appendix C) supersede its original 10(j) 
recommendations.         
65. 
Two of Interior’s recommendations are outside the scope of section 10(j).  The 
first recommendation, is that NYSEG limit the rate of change in impoundment elevation 
to no more than 26 inches per hour in the downward direction and 6 inches per hour in 
the upward direction to support navigation on the Champlain Canal and ensure the 
continuity of downstream flow in the Hudson River during impoundment refill.  Because 
the measure is intended to support navigation and not fish and wildlife resources, it does 
not fall with the scope of section 10(j).  The second recommendation is to install a 
fishway at the project if an upstream fishway is installed at a downstream, non-project 
dam.  Because the measure is conditioned on an uncertain future action, it does not fall 
within the scope of section 10(j).  Both recommendations are discussed in the next 
section.

SECTION 10(a)(1) OF THE FPA 
67. 
Section 10(a)(1) of the FPA33 requires that any project for which the Commission 
issues a license be best adapted to a comprehensive plan for improving or developing a 
waterway or waterways for the use or benefit of interstate or foreign commerce; for the 
improvement and utilization of waterpower development; for the adequate protection, 
mitigation, and enhancement of fish and wildlife; and for other beneficial public uses, 
including irrigation, flood control, water supply, recreation, and other purposes.   
68. 
The following sections discuss two recommendations filed by Interior under 
section 10(j) regarding rates of change in the impoundment elevation to support 
navigation on the Champlain Canal and the conditional future installation of a new 
upstream fishway for blueback herring that are outside the scope of section 10(j), and 
other measures from NYSEG’s proposal, including the Settlement Agreement, and staff’s 
recommendations.  These measures are considered under the broad public interest 
standard of section 10(a)(1) of the FPA.

of the license notes that installation of the upstream fishway may not occur until the 
upstream fishway has been approved by the Commission after the filing of an application 
to amend the license. 
2. 
Post-Licensing Fishway Design Measurements 
74. 
NYSEG proposes to conduct field measurements immediately after the installation 
of any fishways required by the license to confirm that the water velocities, attraction 
flows, and plunge pool depths of such fishways meet FWS’s fish passage engineering 
design criteria that are in place at the time of installation.  There is little benefit to this 
measure because the same information sought by the measure is readily available or 
attainable through other means.  For example, the annual report required to be submitted 
as part of the fishway operation and maintenance plan would include a summary of the 
status of the fishways and their associated flows (including any attraction flows), and the 
approach velocities, attraction flows, and plunge pool depths of each fishway could be 
obtained, or calculated from, the as-built drawings required by Article 207 of the license.  
Nevertheless, the measure is required by the license because it is mandatory under section 
18 of the FPA (prescription 9.4.1) and section 401 of the CWA (certification condition 
9).

PROJECT BOUNDARY   
75. 
Project boundaries enclose the project works that are to be licensed and include 
“only those lands necessary for operation and maintenance of the project and for other 
project purposes, such as recreation, shoreline control, or protection of environmental 
resources.”37  
76. 
The current project boundary encloses the impoundment (to a contour elevation of 
72.6 feet), dam, powerhouse, the upstream portion of Lock C3 (i.e., that portion upstream 
of the project dam), and the transmission line corridor.  NYSEG proposes to expand the 
project boundary by 5.75 acres to include the excavated tailrace channel and its 
accompanying guide walls as well as the earthen embankment located on the east side of 
the river, but does not propose to add the downstream portion of Lock C3 (including the 
downstream miter gates) to the project boundary.   
77. 
Although the upstream miter gates are the primary water retaining feature of Lock 
C3—because they are typically in a closed position—the downstream miter gates also 
serve to maintain the project impoundment in certain situations.  For example, for a 
vessel to pass upstream through the locks, the upstream miter gates must be opened, 
during which time the downstream miter gates remain closed and help maintain the 
impoundment.  Therefore, the entire navigation lock, including both miter gates, serves to 
maintain the project impoundment and is thus integral to the project and its operation and 
should be included in the project boundary.   
78. 
Article 203 requires NYSEG to file a revised Exhibit G drawing with a project 
boundary that encloses the entire Lock C3.

electric service in the future. 
E. 
Need for Power 
97. 
NYSEG serves approximately 900,000 electricity customers across New York.  
The Upper Mechanicville Project has an installed capacity of 16.53 MW and has 
produced an average of about 88,537 megawatt-hours (MWh) of energy annually over 
the period from 2005 to 2017. 
98. 
To assess the need for power, staff looked at the needs in the operating region in 
which the project is located.  Power from the Upper Mechanicville Project would be used 
to support demand in the Northeast Power Coordinating Council – New York region of 
the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC).  The NERC annually 
forecasts electricity supply and demand nationally and regionally for a 10-year period.  
According to NERC’s 2019 long-term reliability assessment, the total peak demand in the 
assessment area is forecasted to decline from 32,063 MW in 2021 to 31,115 MW in 2029.  
The region is also forecasted to have more than necessary excess capacity and meet the 
excess capacity threshold or reference margin level of 15%.  However, the project’s 
power can continue to satisfy NYSEG’s customers’ needs, meet part of the regional need 
for power, and maintain the stability of the power system.

PROJECT ECONOMICS 
102. In determining whether to issue a new license for an existing hydroelectric project, 
the Commission considers several public interest factors, including the economic benefits 
of project power.  Under the Commission’s approach to evaluating the economics of 
hydropower projects, as articulated in Mead Corp.,44 the Commission uses current costs 
to compare the costs of the project and likely alternative power with no forecasts 
concerning potential future inflation, escalation, or deflation beyond the license issuance 
date.  The basic purpose of the Commission’s economic analysis is to provide a general 
estimate of the potential power benefits and the costs of a project, and of reasonable 
alternatives to project power.  The estimate helps to support an informed decision 
concerning what is in the public interest with respect to a proposed license. 
                                                          
44 72 FERC ¶ 61,027 (1995). 
Page 23 of 71
Exhibit __ (CCE-31) - Part D 


--- Page 1229 ---
Project No. 2934-029 
 
- 24 - 
 
 
 
103. In applying this analysis to the Upper Mechanicville Project, three options were 
considered:  no-action, NYSEG’s proposal, and the project as licensed herein.45  Under 
the no-action alternative, the project would continue to operate as it does now.  The 
project has an installed capacity of 16.53 MW and generates an average of 88,537 MWh 
of electricity annually.  The average annual project cost is about $3,754,815, or 
$42.41/MWh.  When an estimate of average generation is multiplied by the alternative 
power cost of $24.83/MWh,46 the total value of the project’s power is $2,198,374 in 2020 
dollars.  To determine whether the project is currently economically beneficial, the 
project’s cost is subtracted from the value of the project’s power.  Therefore, the project 
costs $1,556,441, or $17.58/MWh, more than the likely cost of alternative power. 
104. As proposed by NYSEG, the levelized annual cost of operating the project is 
$5,909,990, or $74.92/MWh.  Based on an estimated average generation of 78,887 MWh 
and the alternative power cost of $25.35/MWh, the total value of the project’s power 
would be $1,999,785.  Therefore, in the first year of operation, the project would cost 
$3,910,205, or $49.57/MWh, more than the likely cost of alternative power. 
105. As licensed herein with mandatory conditions and staff measures, the levelized 
annual cost of operating the project will be about $5,911,502, or $74.94/MWh.  The 
project will generate 78,887 MWh of energy annually and have a power value of 
$1,999,785, or $25.35/MWh.  Therefore, in the first year of operation, the project will 
cost $3,911,717, or $49.59/MWh, more than the likely cost of alternative power. 
106. Although our analysis shows that the project as licensed herein would cost more to 
operate than our estimated cost of alternative power, it is the applicant who must decide 
whether to accept this license and any financial risk that entails. 
107. Although staff does not explicitly account for the effects inflation may have on the 
future cost of electricity, the fact that hydropower generation is relatively insensitive to 
inflation compared to fossil-fueled generators is an important economic consideration for 
power producers and the consumers they serve.  This is one reason project economics is 
only one of the many public interest factors the Commission considers in determining 
whether or not, and under what conditions, to issue a license. 
                                                          
45 Details of Commission staff’s economic analysis for the project as licensed 
herein, and for the other two alternatives, are included in section 4.0 of the EA.  All costs 
were escalated to 2020 dollars.

COMPREHENSIVE DEVELOPMENT 
108. Sections 4(e) and 10(a)(1) of the FPA47 require the Commission to give equal 
consideration to power development purposes and to the purposes of energy 
conservation; the protection, mitigation of damage to, and enhancement of fish and 
wildlife; the protection of recreational opportunities; and the preservation of other aspects 
of environmental quality.  Any license issued must be such as in the Commission’s 
judgment will be best adapted to a comprehensive plan for improving or developing a 
waterway or waterways for all beneficial public uses.  The decision to license this project, 
and the terms and conditions included herein, reflect such consideration. 
109. The EA for the project contains background information, analysis of effects, and 
support for related license articles.  Based on the record of this proceeding, including the 
EA and the comments thereon, licensing the Upper Mechanicville Project, as described in 
this order, would not constitute a major federal action significantly affecting the quality 
of the human environment.  The project will be safe if operated and maintained in 
accordance with the requirements of the license. 
110. Based on Commission staff’s independent review and evaluation of the Upper 
Mechanicville Project, recommendations from the resource agencies and other 
stakeholders, and the no-action alternative, as documented in the EA, the project as 
licensed herein is selected and found to be best adapted to a comprehensive plan for 
improving or developing the Hudson River. 
111. This alternative is selected because:  (1) issuing a new license will serve to 
maintain a beneficial and dependable source of electric energy; (2) the required 
environmental measures will protect or enhance water quality, fish and wildlife 
resources, terrestrial resources, threatened and endangered species, and cultural 
resources; and (3) the 16.53 MW of electric capacity comes from a renewable resource 
that does not contribute to atmospheric pollution.

more than 50 years.

113. On October 19, 2017, the Commission established a 40-year default license term 
policy for original and new licenses, effective as of October 26, 2017.49  The Policy 
Statement provides for exceptions to the 40-year default license term under certain 
circumstances:  (1) establishing a shorter or longer license term if necessary to coordinate 
license terms for projects located in the same river basin; (2) deferring to a shorter or 
longer license term explicitly agreed to in a generally-supported comprehensive 
settlement agreement; and (3) establishing a longer license term upon a showing by the 
license applicant that substantial voluntary measures were either previously implemented 
during the prior license term, or substantial new measures are expected to be 
implemented under the new license.   
114. As previously noted, NYSEG filed a comprehensive Settlement Agreement for the 
project addressing issues related to project operation and the need for license conditions 
that require minimum flows, fish passage and protection, bat and bald eagle protection, 
and invasive species management.  In the the Settlement Agreement, NYSEG, FWS, 
New York DEC, and Trout Unlimited explicitly agree to issuance of a license with a 
50-year term.   Therefore, the second exception applies, and this license is issued for a 
period of 50 years.    
115. Because the term of the current license does not expire until March 31, 2021, this 
license is not effective until April 1, 2021.50   
The Director orders: 
(A) This license is issued to New York State Electric & Gas Corporation 
(licensee), for a period of 50 years, effective April 1, 2021, to operate and maintain the 
Upper Mechanicville Hydroelectric Project.  This license is subject to the terms and 
conditions of the Federal Power Act (FPA), which is incorporated by reference as part of 
the license, and subject to the regulations the Commission issues under the provisions of 
the FPA.

C3); (3) an approximately 550-foot-long earth embankment; (4) a 1.8-mile-long

Article 204.  Amortization Reserve.  Pursuant to section 10(d) of the Federal 
Power Act, a specified reasonable rate of return upon the net investment in the project 
must be used for determining surplus earnings of the project for the establishment and 
maintenance of amortization reserves.  The licensee must set aside in a project 
amortization reserve account at the end of each fiscal year one half of the project surplus 
earnings, if any, in excess of the specified rate of return per annum on the net investment. 
To the extent that there is a deficiency of project earnings below the specified rate of 
return per annum for any fiscal year, the licensee must deduct the amount of that 
deficiency from the amount of any surplus earnings subsequently accumulated, until 
absorbed.  The licensee must set aside one-half of the remaining surplus earnings, if any, 
cumulatively computed, in the project amortization reserve account.  The licensee must 
maintain the amounts established in the project amortization reserve account until further 
order of the Commission.  
The specified reasonable rate of return used in computing amortization reserves 
must be calculated annually based on current capital ratios developed from an average of 
13 monthly balances of amounts properly included in the licensee's long-term debt and 
Page 29 of 71
Exhibit __ (CCE-31) - Part D 


--- Page 1235 ---
Project No. 2934-029 
 
- 30 - 
 
 
 
proprietary capital accounts as listed in the Commission's Uniform System of Accounts. 
The cost rate for such ratios must be the weighted average cost of long-term debt and 
preferred stock for the year, and the cost of common equity must be the interest rate on 
10-year government bonds (reported as the Treasury Department's 10-year constant 
maturity series) computed on the monthly average for the year in question plus four 
percentage points (400 basis points).  
Article 205.  Headwater Benefits.  If the licensee's project was directly benefited 
by the construction work of another licensee, a permittee, or the United States on a 
storage reservoir or other headwater improvement during the term of the original license 
(including extensions of that term by annual licenses), and if those headwater benefits 
were not previously assessed and reimbursed to the owner of the headwater 
improvement, the licensee must reimburse the owner of the headwater improvement for 
those benefits, at such time as they are assessed, in the same manner as for benefits 
received during the term of this new license.  The benefits will be assessed in accordance 
with Part 11, Subpart B, of the Commission's regulations. 
Article 206.  Project Land Rights Progress Report.  No later than four years after 
the effective date of the license, the licensee must file a report with the Commission 
describing the status of acquiring title in fee or the rights for all lands within the project 
boundary.  The report must provide an overview map of each parcel and summary tables 
identifying the licensee’s rights over each parcel within the project boundary.  The report 
must also include specific supporting documentation showing the status of the land rights 
on all parcels of land within the project boundary that:  (1) have been acquired up to the 
date of filing the report, including pertinent deeds, lease agreements, and/or bill of sale 
information that specifically verify the licensee’s rights; and (2) the licensee’s plan and 
schedule for acquiring rights to all remaining project lands prior to the five-year deadline, 
including a history of actions taken, current owner information, the type of rights to be 
acquired whether in fee or by easement, and the timeline for completing property 
acquisition.  
Article 207.  As-built Drawings.  Within 90 days of completion of construction of 
the facilities authorized by this license, the licensee must file for Commission approval, 
revised Exhibits A, F, and G, as applicable, to describe and show those project facilities 
as built.  If the licensee determines the previously approved exhibits reflect the as-built 
facilities and no revisions are necessary, the licensee must file a letter stating the 
approved exhibits reflect the as-built project facilities.

Article 402.  Project Operation.  The licensee must operate the project in 
accordance with the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation’s (New 
York DEC) certification (Appendix A), which specifies the required mode of operation 
(run-of-river) (condition 7), seasonal minimum flow (condition 8), and allowable 
impoundment elevations and rates of change in impoundment elevation (conditions 7 and 
17). 
The run-of-river, seasonal minimum flow, and impoundment elevation 
requirements may be temporarily modified as follows: 
Planned Deviations 
Requirements regarding run-of-river operation, impoundment elevations, rates of 
change in impoundment elevation, and the seasonal minimum flow may be temporarily 
modified for short periods, of up to 3 weeks, after mutual agreement among the licensee 
and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and New York DEC (collectively, resource 
agencies).  After concurrence from the resource agencies, the licensee must notify the 
Commission within 14 days and file a report with the Secretary of the Commission as 
soon as possible, but no later than 30 days after the onset of the planned deviation.  Each 
report must include:  (1) the reasons for the deviation and how project operations were 
modified; (2) the duration and magnitude of the deviation; (3) any observed or reported 
environmental effects; and (4) documentation of consultation with the resource agencies.  
For planned deviations exceeding 3 weeks, the licensee must file an application for a 
temporary amendment of the operational requirements of this license and receive 
Commission approval prior to implementation. 
 
 
 
Unplanned Deviations 
 
Requirements regarding run-of-river operation, impoundment elevations, rates of 
change in impoundment elevation, and the seasonal minimum flow may be temporarily 
modified if required by operating emergencies beyond the control of the licensee (i.e., 
unplanned deviations).  For any unplanned deviation from run-of-river operation or 
deviation in impoundment elevation or minimum flow that lasts longer than 3 hours or 
results in visible environmental effects such as a fish kill, the licensee must notify the 
resource agencies within 24 hours, and the Commission within 14 days, and file a report 
as soon as possible, but no later than 30 days after each such incident.  The report must 
include:  (1) the cause of the deviation; (2) the duration and magnitude of the deviation; 
(3) any pertinent operational and/or monitoring data; (4) a timeline of the incident and the 
licensee’s response; (5) any comments or correspondence received from the resource 
agencies, or confirmation that no comments were received from the resource agencies; 
Page 33 of 71
Exhibit __ (CCE-31) - Part D 


--- Page 1239 ---
Project No. 2934-029 
 
- 34 - 
 
 
 
(6) documentation of any observed or reported environmental effects; and (7) a 
description of measures implemented to prevent similar deviations in the future.   
 
For unplanned deviations from run-of-river operation, impoundment elevations, or 
minimum flow lasting 3 hours or less that do not result in visible environmental effects, 
the licensee must include in the annual operation compliance monitoring report required 
by Article 403, a description of each incident that occurred during the prior October 1 
through September 30 time period.  The report must include for each 3 hours or less 
deviation:  (1) the cause of the deviation; (2) the duration and magnitude of the deviation; 
(3) any pertinent operational and/or monitoring data; (4) a timeline of the incident and the 
licensee’s response to each deviation; (5) any comments or correspondence received from 
the resource agencies, or confirmation that no comments were received from the resource 
agencies; and (6) a description of measures implemented to prevent similar deviations in 
the future.

Article 406.  Use and Occupancy.  (a) In accordance with the provisions of this 
article, the licensee must have the authority to grant permission for certain types of use 
and occupancy of project lands and waters and to convey certain interests in project lands 
and waters for certain types of use and occupancy, without prior Commission approval.  
The licensee may exercise the authority only if the proposed use and occupancy is 
consistent with the purposes of protecting and enhancing the scenic, recreational, and 
other environmental values of the project.  For those purposes, the licensee must also 
have continuing responsibility to supervise and control the use and occupancies for which 
it grants permission, and to monitor the use of, and ensure compliance with the covenants 
of the instrument of conveyance for, any interests that it has conveyed, under this article.  
If a permitted use and occupancy violates any condition of this article or any other 
condition imposed by the licensee for protection and enhancement of the project's scenic, 
recreational, or other environmental values, or if a covenant of a conveyance made under 
the authority of this article is violated, the licensee must take any lawful action necessary 
to correct the violation.  For a permitted use or occupancy, that action includes, if 
necessary, canceling the permission to use and occupy the project lands and waters and 
requiring the removal of any non-complying structures and facilities. 
 
(b) The type of use and occupancy of project lands and waters for which the 
licensee may grant permission without prior Commission approval are:  (1) landscape 
plantings; (2) non-commercial piers, landings, boat docks, or similar structures and 
facilities that can accommodate no more than 10 water craft at a time and where said 
facility is intended to serve single-family type dwellings; (3) embankments, bulkheads, 
retaining walls, or similar structures for erosion control to protect the existing shoreline; 
and (4) food plots and other wildlife enhancement.  To the extent feasible and desirable to 
protect and enhance the project's scenic, recreational, and other environmental values, the 
licensee must require multiple use and occupancy of facilities for access to project lands 
or waters.  The licensee must also ensure, to the satisfaction of the Commission's 
authorized representative, that the use and occupancies for which it grants permission are 
maintained in good repair and comply with applicable state and local health and safety 
requirements.  Before granting permission for construction of bulkheads or retaining 
walls, the licensee must:  (1) inspect the site of the proposed construction, (2) consider 
whether the planting of vegetation or the use of riprap would be adequate to control 
erosion at the site, and (3) determine that the proposed construction is needed and would 
not change the basic contour of the impoundment shoreline.  To implement this 
paragraph (b), the licensee may, among other things, establish a program for issuing 
permits for the specified types of use and occupancy of project lands and waters, which 
may be subject to the payment of a reasonable fee to cover the licensee's costs of 
administering the permit program.  The Commission reserves the right to require the 
licensee to file a description of its standards, guidelines, and procedures for implementing 
this paragraph (b) and to require modification of those standards, guidelines, or 
procedures.

(c)  The licensee may convey easements or rights-of-way across, or leases of

drains and water mains; (3) sewers that do not discharge into project waters; (4) minor 
access roads; (5) telephone, gas, and electric utility distribution lines; (6) non-project 
overhead electric transmission lines that do not require erection of support structures 
within the project boundary; (7) submarine, overhead, or underground major telephone 
distribution cables or major electric distribution lines (69-kV or less); and (8) water 
intake or pumping facilities that do not extract more than one million gallons per day 
from a project impoundment.  No later than January 31 of each year, the licensee must

the lands subject to the conveyance, and the nature of the use for which the interest was 
conveyed.  No report filing is required if no conveyances were made under paragraph (c) 
during the previous calendar year.  
 
(d)  The licensee may convey fee title to, easements or rights-of-way across, or 
leases of project lands for:  (1) construction of new bridges or roads for which all 
necessary state and federal approvals have been obtained; (2) sewer or effluent lines that 
discharge into project waters, for which all necessary federal and state water quality 
certification or permits have been obtained; (3) other pipelines that cross project lands or 
waters but do not discharge into project waters; (4) non-project overhead electric 
transmission lines that require erection of support structures within the project boundary, 
for which all necessary federal and state approvals have been obtained; (5) private or 
public marinas that can accommodate no more than 10 water craft at a time and are 
located at least one-half mile (measured over project waters) from any other private or 
public marina; (6) recreational development consistent with an approved report on 
recreational resources of an Exhibit E; and (7) other uses, if:  (i) the amount of land 
conveyed for a particular use is five acres or less; (ii) all of the land conveyed is located 
at least 75 feet, measured horizontally, from project waters at normal surface elevation; 
and (iii) no more than 50 total acres of project lands for each project development are 
conveyed under this clause (d)(7) in any calendar year.  At least 60 days before 
conveying any interest in project lands under this paragraph (d), the licensee must file a 
letter with the Commission, stating its intent to convey the interest and briefly describing 
the type of interest and location of the lands to be conveyed (a marked Exhibit G map 
may be used), the nature of the proposed use, the identity of any federal or state agency 
official consulted, and any federal or state approvals required for the proposed use.  
Unless the Commission's authorized representative, within 45 days from the filing date, 
requires the licensee to file an application for prior approval, the licensee may convey the 
intended interest at the end of that period.

Article 1. The entire project, as described in this order of the Commission, shall 
be subject to all of the provisions, terms, and conditions of the license.  
Article 2. No substantial change shall be made in the maps, plans, specifications,
