theretofore made a part of the license as may be specified by the Commission.  
Article 3. The project area and project works shall be in substantial conformity 
with the approved exhibits referred to in Article 2 herein or as changed in accordance 
with the provisions of said article. Except when emergency shall require for the 
protection of navigation, life, health, or property, there shall not be made without prior 
approval of the Commission any substantial alteration or addition not in conformity with 
the approved plans to any dam or other project works under the license or any substantial 
use of project lands and waters not authorized herein; and any emergency alteration, 
addition, or use so made shall thereafter be subject to such modification and change as 
the Commission may direct. Minor changes in project works, or in uses of project lands 
and waters, or divergence from such approved exhibits may be made if such changes will 
not result in a decrease in efficiency, in a material increase in cost, in an adverse 
environmental impact, or in impairment of the general scheme of development; but any 
of such minor changes made without the prior approval of the Commission, which in its 
judgment have produced or will produce any of such results, shall be subject to such 
alteration as the Commission may direct.

Regulatory Commission (FERC) for FERC Project # 2934.

Environmental Conservation (DEC) hereby certifies: 
 
 
The DEC has reviewed the certificate holder’s Application for Federal 
Hydroelectric License (hereafter referred to as “the Application”) and 
all other available pertinent information, including the Offer of 
Settlement dated February 19, 2020; 
 
The Project will comply with Sections 301, 302, 303, 306, and 307 of 
the Federal Water Pollution Control Act as amended and as 
implemented by the limitations, standards and criteria of the state 
statutory and regulatory requirements set forth in 6NYCRR Section 
608.9(a); and 
 
The Project will comply with applicable New York State effluent 
limitations, water quality standards and thermal discharge criteria set 
forth in 6NYCRR Parts 700-706. 
 
3. 
Conformance with Plans.  All activities authorized by this permit must 
be in strict conformance with the approved plans submitted by the applicant or 
applicant's agent as part of the permit application.  Such approved plans were 
prepared by HDR and include the Offer of Settlement and associated 
implementation schedules dated February 19, 2020.  
 
4. 
Offer of Settlement.  This certificate includes and incorporates the 
provisions of the Upper Mechanicville Hydroelectric Project Offer of Settlement 
(“Settlement”) dated February 19, 2020, to the extent that the Settlement provides 
for or requires the certificate holder to comply with New York State water quality 
standards and the conditions of this certificate.    
 
5.

emergency provisions described in the Settlement Agreement, the following

10.

locations and methods shall be developed in consultation with the DEC.

accomplished according to a protocol that is consistent with DEC’s Technical and 
Operations Guidance (TOGS) 5.1.9 or applicable guidelines/regulations.  The 
sampling protocol shall include a disposal protocol based on analytical sediment 
sampling results and current applicable regulations/guidelines.  The sampling results 
are required to be submitted to the DEC at least 45 days prior to the commencement 
of dredging or work that will disturb sediment in the project waters.  Dredging and 
other excavation can not commence until the certificate holder also secures the 
DEC’s approval for the disposal or interim holding locations for any sediments to be 
removed from the project waters.

8.

Pursuant to Section 18 of the Federal Power Act, the Secretary of the Interior

fishways described in the Department of Interior’s Prescription for Fishways  
 
at the Upper Mechanicville Hydroelectric Project. 
 
9. 
MODIFIED PRESCRIPTION FOR FISHWAYS 
 
Pursuant to Section 18 of the Federal Power Act, as amended, the Secretary of the 
Department of the Interior, as delegated to the Service, proposes to exercise his authority 
to prescribe the construction, operation and maintenance of such fishways as deemed 
necessary, subject to the procedural provisions contained above. 
 
The Service’s Modified Prescription reflects a number of issues and concerns related to 
fish restoration and passage that have been raised by the Licensee, Commission staff, 
State resource agencies, and other parties involved in these proceedings. 
 
Fishways shall be constructed, operated, and maintained at the Licensee’s expense to 
provide safe, timely and effective passage for the catadromous American eel.  The fish 
protection and downstream passage facilities should also benefit anadromous species 
such as the Blueback Herring, Alewife, and American shad, as well as resident riverine 
fish species.  The provision for future upstream passage for anadromous species will 
allow for improvements in the future as part of a basinwide approach. 
 
To ensure the immediate and timely contribution of fishways to the ongoing and future 
fish enhancement programs in the Hudson River, the following are included and shall be 
incorporated by the Licensee to ensure the effectiveness of the fishways pursuant to 
Section 1701(b) of the 1992 National Energy Policy Act (P.L. 102-486, Title XVII, 106 
Stat. 3008).

9.1 
Design Populations 
 
9.1.1 American Eel 
 
While the Service does not have a precise estimate of the numbers of eels that would be 
expected to use fish passage facilities at the Project, such passage would enhance the eel 
stocks and help achieve overall management goals.  In addition, upstream passage needs 
for eels differ from those of Blueback Herring and other anadromous species.  Separate 
upstream eel ladders are typically installed at barriers in addition to those provided for 
anadromous fish.  The eel ladder prescribed herein should adequately handle any 
anticipated eel movements. 
 
9.1.2 Other Species 
 
There are no design populations for other fish species expected to utilize the fishways.  
However, the prescribed downstream fish passage system should be capable of handling 
any anticipated movement by any fish species that may use the fishways. 
 
9.2 
Operational Flows 
 
Upstream and downstream fishways shall be operated during the designated migration 
period (currently April 1 through November 30 for upstream passage and ice-out through 
November 30 for downstream passage) at all times under all river flows up to the 
maximum capacity of the fishways.1 
 
9.3 
Scheduling 
 
9.3.1 Construction Schedule 
 
The timely installation of prescribed fishway structures, facilities, or devices is a measure 
directly related to those structures, facilities, or devices and is necessary to ensure the 
effectiveness of such structures, facilities, or devices.  Therefore, the Service’s Modified 
Prescription includes the express requirements that the Licensee (1) notify, and (2) obtain 
approval from, the Service for any extensions of time to comply with the provisions 
included in the Service’s Modified Prescription.  The installation of fishway structures 
and other measures should comply with the following schedule:

9.3.2 Operational Schedule 
 
Regarding the timing of seasonal fishway operations, fishways shall be maintained and 
operated, at the Licensee’s expense, to maximize fish passage effectiveness throughout 
the upstream and downstream migration periods specifically for American Eel, although 
the other fish species will benefit from the exclusion and downstream passage measures 
for American Eel.  The upstream passage facilities will initially be operated from April 1 
through November 30 of each year, while the downstream passage facilities will operate 
from ice-out through November 30 of each year.  The fishways are to operate whenever 
generation occurs during the migration period, which is expected to be nearly 100% of 
the time.  During the term of the license, the Service, in consultation with the NYSDEC 
and the Licensee, may modify windows for specific fishway facilities based on 
monitoring data or other new information that becomes available.    
 
9.4 
Operational Procedures 
 
The Licensee shall keep the fishways in proper order and shall keep fishway areas clear 
of trash, logs, and material that would hinder passage.  Anticipated maintenance shall be 
performed sufficiently before a migratory period such that fishways can be tested and 
inspected, and will operate effectively prior to and during the migratory periods.  The 
Licensee should develop a Fishway Operation and Maintenance Plan (FOMP), in 
consultation with the Service and the NYSDEC, to document regular maintenance 
activities and emergency procedures.  The FOMP will include general schedules and 
procedures for the following: 
 
 Seasonal installation, operation, and maintenance of an eel ladder and collection 
tank, and release of any captured eels upstream of the dam; 
 Installation and maintenance of 3/4”-clear-spaced trashracks or the equivalent fish 
exclusion measures (e.g., an overlay or other screening type system); 
 Seasonal operation and maintenance of the downstream fish passage structures 
including an attraction flow provided through the passage structure and a plunge

pool downstream of the passage structure; and 
 Annual reporting and emergency exceptions. 
 
9.4.1 Effectiveness Testing 
 
The Licensee will conduct field measurements associated with the downstream American 
Eel passage immediately after installation of the alternative downstream passage path to 
ensure compliance with the Service criteria performance standards for water velocities, 
attraction flows, plunge pool depths, and all other criteria.  Any necessary modifications 
will be made to the facility to meet compliance with the Service Criteria at the time of 
approval of the final designs for the measure.    
 
The Licensee will conduct field measurements associated with the eel ladder immediately 
after installation to ensure compliance with the Service Criteria performance standards 
for water velocities, attraction flows, and all other criteria.  Any necessary modifications 
will be made to the facility to meet compliance with the Service Criteria at the time of 
approval of the final designs for the measure.     
 
If the design of the upstream fish passage structure deviates from the Service Criteria, the 
Licensee will conduct effectiveness testing of the future upstream fish passage structure 
to ensure compliance with the Service Criteria.  In addition, the Licensee will perform 
field measurements to ensure compliance with performance standards for water 
velocities, attraction flows, and all other criteria.  Any necessary modifications will be 
made to the facility to meet compliance with Service Criteria at the time of approval of 
the final designs for the fishway. 
 
The Licensee will submit reports of all field measurements and effectiveness testing to 
the Service and the NYSDEC within 9 months of structure installation, and to the 
Commission within 12 months of structure installation.

9.7 
Fish Passage Facilities 
 
9.7.1 Downstream Passage Facilities 
The licensee should install a new trashrack with a maximum clear spacing of ¾”.  The 
trashrack should cover the intake area.  The maximum approach velocity, as measured 1 
foot in front of the intake should be 2 feet per second.  The Licensee should submit its 
conceptual/preliminary downstream passage design to the Service and the NYSDEC for 
review by October 31, 2021.  The design should comply with the applicable Service 
design criteria and standards.  The 60% design should be submitted to the Service and 
NYSDEC for review by April 30, 2023, and the final design should be submitted to the 
Service and the NYSDEC for review and approval by October 31, 2023.  The approved 
designs should be filed with FERC by December 31, 2023.      
 
The downstream fish passage structure should consist of a sluice-gate, a low-level 
(submerged) intake for American eel passage, and a plunge pool to be developed in 
consultation with, and approved by, the Service and NYSDEC.  The sluice must be free 
of any rough edges or obstructions and the plunge pool must be at least 1 foot deep for 
every 4 feet of drop, of 4 feet deep, whichever is greater.  A continuous flow of at least 
5% of the maximum hydraulic capacity of the Project (600 cubic feet per second) should 
be provided at all times during the downstream passage season, unless an alternative flow 
is approved by the Service and the NYSDEC.     
9.7.2 Upstream Passage Facilities – American Eel 
The Licensee has proposed to install a spiral eel ramp.  The design of the seasonal eel 
ramp will be developed in consultation with the USFWS and the NYSDEC, based on 
preliminary designs provided in the Licensee’s November 29, 2019, filing in response to 
the Commission’s Additional Information Request (NYSEG 2019b).  The ramp will 
include a colletion facility near the exit where the eels will be captured and transported to 
an agree-upon upstream location to avoid entrainment back through the turbines of 
fallback over the dam.  A solid cover will be installed to minimize predation and to 
exclude external light sources.  The 60% design should be provided to the Service and 
NYSDEC for review by October 31, 2021, and the final designs should be provided to 
the Service and NYSDEC for review and approval by Janurary 31, 2022.  The approved 
design should be filed with the Commission by March 31, 2022.

3.0 
MEASURES THAT THE PARTIES AGREE SHOULD BE

3.1 
Project Operations 
3.1.1 General Agreements  
Upon the issuance and acceptance of the new license, or the Effective Date of the 
new license, whichever is later, and consistent with the Project’s existing license issued 
by the Commission on April 23, 1981, the Licensee shall operate the Project in a 
run-of-river mode as modified in support of NYSCC’s navigation activities. 
Project operations will be influenced by the NYSCC’s navigation and non-
navigation seasons, which will be defined by the NYSCC.  During the navigation season, 
the Licensee will maintain the impoundment at an elevation of 72 inches or greater above 
the Project’s fixed spillway, which equates to an elevation of 72.6 feet (NGVD29), unless 
directed by the NYSCC or due to conditions as defined in Section 3.1.2 of this Offer of 
Settlement.  However, given the potential frequency of elevation adjustments that can be 
requested by NYSCC and the variability in river hydrology, for the purposes of 
compliance reporting, the Licensee will be allowed to return the impoundment to 72 
inches or greater above the Project’s fixed spillway at the Licensee’s discretion.  In 
addition, during the navigation season, the Parties agree that only when the impoundment 
drops in excess of six inches from the target elevation of 72 inches above the Project’s 
fixed spillway (unless directed by the NYSCC or in the process of returning the 
impoundment level to 72 inches above the Project’s fixed spillway) shall a notification to 
the Commission and the NYSDEC be required.  If such notification is required, the 
Licensee shall notify NYSDEC as soon as possible by phone or email, but no later than 
five (5) business days after any such deviation.  The Licensee shall notify the 
Commission consistent with requirements established by the Commission. 
 
During the non-navigation season, the Licensee shall at all times make a good 
faith effort to keep the impoundment elevation at an elevation of 72 inches or greater 
above the Project’s fixed spillway, which equates to an elevation of 72.6 feet (NGVD29), 
Page 61 of 71
Exhibit __ (CCE-31) - Part D 


--- Page 1267 ---
Project No. 2934-029 
 
- 62 - 
 
 
 
unless directed by the NYSCC or due to conditions as defined in Section 3.1.2 of this 
Offer of Settlement.  The parties agree that only when the impoundment drops in excess 
of 6 inches from the target elevation 72 inches above the Project’s fixed spillway (unless 
directed by the NYSCC) shall a notification to the Commission and the NYSDEC be

Unless directed otherwise by the NYSCC or due to conditions as defined in

by this Offer of Settlement nor should they be conditioned by the license to be issued by 
the Commission. 
 
 
Related to the operations of the NYSCC, the Parties agree that neither this Offer of 
Settlement nor the new license to be issued by the Commission shall have any influence 
on the NYSCC, NYSCC operations, or navigational activities associated with the Project.  
 
3.1.2 Exceptions 
Project operations as defined by Section 3.1.1 of this Offer of Settlement may be 
curtailed or suspended if required by operating emergency or as directed by the NYSCC.

In addition, Project Operations as defined in Section 3.1.1 may be curtailed or suspended 
upon prior mutual agreement between the Licensee and the NYSDEC.  In the event of 
any operating emergency beyond the control of the Licensee, the Project Operations as 
defined in Section 3.1.1 may be curtailed or suspended for the time period necessary to 
rectify such condition.  The Licensee shall notify the NYSDEC by phone call or email as 
soon as possible, but no later than five (5) business days after any such operating 
emergency or receipt of direction from the NYSCC.  The Licensee shall notify the 
Commission consistent with requirements established by the Commission. 
3.1.3 Justification 
The Parties understand that the Project is located adjacent to NYSCC’s Lock C-3, 
which supports navigation associated with the Hudson River (Champlain Canal).  Due to 
the railroad bridge located approximately 0.55 mile upstream of Lock C-3, the NYSCC 
routinely directs the Licensee to adjust the impoundment elevation to accommodate the 
safe passage of vessels through the Project’s impoundment as to provide adequate 
mast/vessel clearance under the bridge.  In addition, NYSCC directs the Licensee to raise 
the impoundment to allow for deeper draft vessels to pass through the impoundment.  In 
addition to navigation, in support of the larger Champlain Canal system, NYSCC directs 
impoundment level adjustments to support maintenance, inspections, emergencies, and 
construction activities of the NYSCC.  Based on the studies and consultation performed 
in support of the relicensing, the Parties understand and agree that adjustments to the 
impoundment elevation are necessary in support of the NYSCC activities.  Based on this 
understanding, the Parties have worked to define and differentiate Project operations for 
both the navigation season and the non-navigation season and believe that the agreements 
presented in Section 3.1.1 of this Offer of Settlement provide the best approach for 
addressing the navigational, hydropower, and aquatic resources associated with the 
Project. 
 
          The Parties also understand that based on years of historic joint operations of the 
Project and Lock C-3 in support of navigation, changes in impoundment elevations at a 
rate of 26 inches per hour in the downward direction and 6 inches per hour in the upward 
direction provide a balance between navigation and the aquatic resources associated with 
the Project.  In particular, these rates of change provide the responsiveness needed by the 
NYSCC to coordinate the in-sequence lockages that are required to coordinate the 
passage of boat traffic through the Champlain Canal (i.e., vessels moving both upstream 
[north bound] and downstream [south bound] through Locks C-2, C-3, and C-4).  In 
Page 63 of 71
Exhibit __ (CCE-31) - Part D 


--- Page 1269 ---
Project No. 2934-029 
 
- 64 - 
 
 
 
addition, these rates of changes ensure that the Project provides the desired continuous 
minimum year-round flows downstream of the Project during refill.  
3.2 
Bypass Flow 
 
3.2.1 General Agreements 
 
 
Within 1 month of the issuance and acceptance of the new license, or the Effective 
Date of the new license, whichever is later, and on an annual basis from April 1 to 
November 30, the Licensee shall provide a minimum release of 45 cubic feet per second 
(cfs) or inflow to the Project, whichever is less, to the Project’s bypassed reach.  The 
bypass flow will be provided through flow over the Project’s spillway, flow through the 
Project’s intake bypass sluice gate, flow through the downstream fishway, when 
applicable, as defined in Section 3.3.1.3 of this Offer of Settlement, and/or by other 
means as determined by the Licensee. 
 
3.2.2 Exceptions 
Bypass flow as defined by Section 3.2.1 of this Offer of Settlement may be 
curtailed or suspended if required by operating emergency or as directed by the NYSCC. 
In addition, bypass flow as defined in Section 3.2.1 may be curtailed or suspended upon 
prior mutual agreement between the Licensee and the NYSDEC and the USFWS.  In the 
event of any operating emergency beyond the control of the Licensee, Project Operations 
as defined in Section 3.2.1 may be curtailed or suspended for the time period necessary to 
rectify such condition.  The Licensee shall notify the NYSDEC and the USFWS by 
phone call or email as soon as possible, but no later than five (5) business days after any 
such operating emergency or receipt of direction from the NYSCC.  The Licensee shall 
notify the Commission consistent with requirements established by the Commission. 
3.2.3 Justification 
 
Based on the studies performed in support of the relicensing process, the Parties 
agree that on a seasonal basis, there is a benefit of providing a continuous flow of water 
to the area immediately downstream of the Project’s spillway.  As compared to keeping 
this area inundated, the Parties agree that maintaining a continuous flow through this 
immediate downstream area will benefit aquatic species that may attempt to use the area 
for spawning or nesting habitat. 
 
This Offer of Settlement does not require the Licensee to monitor or test the 
effectiveness of the bypass flow on any species, aquatic habitat, or water quality.

3.3 
Fish Passage and Protection 
 
3.3.1 General Agreements 
 
3.3.1.1 Seasonal Upstream American Eel Ladder 
By the 2023 upstream migration season for American eel, on a seasonal basis, the 
Licensee will install a single ladder for the upstream movement of American eel in the 
Project’s tailrace (river right, looking downstream).  The seasonal eel ladder will be 
installed and operated by April 1 of each year, and will be removed or closed on or after 
November 30 of each year.  The installation, removal and/or closure of the seasonal 
ladder will be performed when river flows and conditions allow for the safe execution of 
such activities.  If river flows or safety conditions prevent the installation and operation 
of the seasonal ladder by April 1st, or require the removal or closure of the ladder prior to 
November 30th, the Licensee will notify the NYSDEC and the USFWS within five (5) 
business days, and such information will be documented in the Fishway Operation and 
Maintenance Report (FOMR) as defined in Section 3.3.3 of this Offer of Settlement. 
The design of the seasonal upstream eel ladder will be based on the conceptual 
design presented in Attachment C to this Offer of Settlement and will be further designed 
and developed in consultation with the USFWS and the NYSDEC.  The ladder will 
terminate in a trap, and eels will be transported and released (e.g., manually or through an 
automated system) at a site to be determined in consultation with the NYSDEC and the 
USFWS during the final design phase.  The Licensee will provide the USFWS and the 
NYSDEC with a final design for the upstream eel ladder prior to April 2022 and will file 
a copy of the design with the Commission within two months of approval by the USFWS 
and the NYSDEC.  The ease of installation to adverse effects from high flows will be 
considered in the design.  The final designs must be approved by the USFWS and the 
NYSDEC. 
This Offer of Settlement does not require the Licensee to perform any monitoring 
of the upstream passage of American eel or the effectiveness of the upstream eel passage 
measures included in the Offer of Settlement.  However, the Licensee will keep accurate 
records of the number of eels captured in the trap and include this information in the 
annual FOMR, as defined in Section 3.3.3 of this Offer of Settlement.  In addition, the 
Licensee, after consultation with the NYSDEC and the USFWS, will make any 
modifications deemed necessary to ensure effective upstream passage of American eel.

3.3.1.2  Seasonal Upstream Fish Passage 
Within one year following the installation of upstream passage facilities at the 
downstream Mechanicville Project (FERC Project No. 6032), passage for the upstream 
migration of fish species within the Hudson River will be installed.  The upstream 
passage will be designed in consultation with, and through approval by, the USFWS and 
the NYSDEC.  In support of meeting the agreed-upon schedule, the USFWS and the 
NYSDEC will notify NYSEG four years prior to the required date for installing the 
upstream fishway at the Upper Mechanicville Project.  If it is not possible to provide at 
least 4 years’ advance notification, the installation date at Upper Mechanicville may be 
delayed upon agreement among the Licensee, the USFWS, and the NYSDEC. 
3.3.1.3  American Eel Exclusion and Downstream Passage 
By September 30, 2025, the Licensee, in consultation with, and through approval 
by, the USFWS and the NYSDEC, will reduce the Project’s existing trashrack clear 
spacing of 5.5-inches to trashrack clear spacing of 0.75-inch.  In addition, by September 
30, 2025, the Licensee, in consultation with, and through approval by, the USFWS and 
the NYSDEC, will provide an alternative path for downstream passage of American eels, 
including appropriate attraction flows (e.g., currently estimated at 600 cfs when the 
Project is operating at maximum hydraulic capacity).  The alternative path for 
downstream passage will be designed to meet the USFWS’ Fish Passage Engineering 
Design Criteria1 at the time of the design effort.  When the Project’s existing trashrack 
spacing is reduced, downstream passage will be provided annually following ice out 
through November 30.  Consistent with USFWS Criteria, site-specific design criteria will 
be applied and considered during the design and approval of the measures. 
3.3.2 Reservation of Authority 
 
In addition to the protection measures outlined in this section, the DOI will reserve 
its authority under Section 18 of the FPA to prescribe additional upstream or downstream 
fishway facilities in the future.  This reservation ensures that adequate facilities for fish 
passage will be in place should management goals or needs change during the term of the 
license.

3.3.3 Fishway Operation and Maintenance Plan 
 
Within 24 months of the issuance and acceptance of the new license, or the 
Effective Date of the new license, whichever is later, the Licensee shall provide a 
Fishway Operation and Maintenance Plan (FOMP) for approval by the USFWS and the 
NYSDEC.  The FOMP will include:  a description of fishway measures associated with 
the Project, an implementation schedule for the fishways, and operation and maintenance 
procedures.  Within 2 months of approval of the FOMP by the NYSDEC and the 
USFWS, the Licensee will file the FOMP with the Commission.  The FOMP will be 
updated as needed in consultation with the USFWS and the NYSDEC and all updates 
will be filed with the Commission.  
Annually, the Licensee will prepare a Fishway Operation and Maintenance Report 
(FOMR) and submit it to the USFWS and the NYSDEC by February 28, and filed with 
the Commission by April 30, beginning with the first full calendar year following filing 
of the FOMP with the Commission.  The FOMR will be in a letter report format and will 
include a summary of the current state of the fishways (structures, flows, etc.) and a 
yearly fishway operation and maintenance report (deviations, issues, timing of 
installation, etc.), as well as the counts of eels captured and released upstream, when 
performed manually, or if available with an automated system and required during the 
design phase. The FOMR will also include any newly available fisheries data obtained or 
collected by the Licensee. The FOMR will reference the FOMP and will provide an 
assessment of any necessary or recommended changes to the FOMP. 
3.3.4 Fishway Effectiveness Testing 
The Licensee will conduct field measurements associated with the upstream eel 
ladder and downstream American eel passage immediately after installation of the each 
measure to ensure compliance with the USFWS Criteria performance standards for water 
velocities, attraction flows, plunge pool depths, and all other criteria.  Any necessary 
modifications will be made to the facilities to ensure compliance with the USFWS 
Criteria in place at the time of approval of the final designs for the measure.   
The Licensee will conduct field measurements of the future upstream fish passage 
structure to ensure compliance with the USFWS Criteria, including compliance with 
performance standards for water velocities, attraction flows, plunge pool depths, and all 
other criteria.  If deemed necessary through consultation between the USFWS, the 
NYSDEC, and the Licensee, effectiveness testing of the facility may be required.  Any 
necessary modifications will be made to the facility to ensure compliance with the 
USFWS criteria in place at the time of approval of the final designs for the fishway.

The Licensee will submit reports of all field measurements and effectiveness

3.3.5 Exceptions 
The Licensee may curtail or suspend fish passage measures for durations less than 
12 hours without notification or reporting to the USFWS and the NYSDEC for general 
maintenance activities needed to facilitate safe and effective passage (e.g., debris removal 
from the sluice gate and/or plunge pool).  In addition, the Licensee may curtail or 
suspend fish protection and passage measures upon prior mutual agreement between the 
Licensee, the USFWS, and the NYSDEC.  In the event of any operating emergency 
beyond the control of the Licensee, the Licensee may curtail or suspend fish protection 
and passage measures for the time period necessary to rectify such an operating 
emergency.  The Licensee shall notify the NYSDEC and the USFWS as soon as possible 
by phone or email, but no later than five (5) business days after any such operating 
emergency.  Any curtailment or suspension of fish passage activities will be documented 
in the FOMR as defined in Section 3.3.3 of this Offer of Settlement.  The Licensee shall 
notify the Commission consistent with requirements established by the Commission. 
3.3.6 Justification 
The lock structures associated with each of the downstream projects are providing 
a means for some fish to migrate to the Upper Mechanicville Project.  In addition, the 
downstream Green Island Project (FERC Project No. 13), is under a Commission 
Compliance Order to complete upstream passage facilities (eel ladders and fish lifts) by 
the end of 2021.  The Parties agree that Lock C-3, located adjacent to the Project, is also 
providing the means for some fish to migrate upstream of the Project.  Therefore, the 
existing river-wide system is providing an opportunity for some fish to migrate upstream 
of the Project.  However, the Parties also agree that over the proposed 50-year term of the 
Project’s new license, upstream migration may be improved.  Therefore, given the 
presence of Lock C-3 on river left, the Parties believe that the installation of a seasonal 
ladder to promote the upstream migration of American eel on river right would be 
beneficial to the species.  This location is consistent with the surveys performed in 
support of the relicensing and thus the Parties agree to the installation of a seasonal eel 
ladder in the Project’s tailrace.   
Regarding upstream passage for other seasonal upstream migrating species, the 
Parties agree that following the installation of potential upstream passage at the 
downstream Mechanicville Project, additional upstream passage at the Upper 
Page 68 of 71
Exhibit __ (CCE-31) - Part D 


--- Page 1274 ---
Project No. 2934-029 
 
- 69 - 
 
 
 
Mechanicville Project may be required.  Therefore, the Parties agree that within one year 
of upstream fish passage being installed at the Mechanicville Project, similar upstream 
passage will be installed at the Upper Mechanicville Project.  
Regarding downstream fish passage and protection, the Parties agree that the 
Project’s two large, slow-moving turbines, in combination with the Project’s lower head 
design, provide a more fish-friendly option for many of the fish that pass through the 
Project’s intake and turbines than other sites in the watershed.  Due to this unique design 
feature, the Parties agree that the Project is considered less detrimental to many of the 
fish species associated with the Hudson River and the Project area than other sites in the 
watershed.  However, due to a lack of Project-specific data, in combination with the 
NYSDEC’s goal of 98% survivability of American eels passing downstream of the 
Project, the Parties have concluded that American eels must be excluded from the 
Project’s intake and passed downstream using measures consistent with the USFWS’ 
Fish Passage Engineering Design Criteria. 
3.4 
Stream Flow and Water Level Monitoring Plan 
3.4.1 General Agreements 
The Licensee shall develop and maintain a Stream Flow and Water Level 
Monitoring Plan (Monitoring Plan) in consultation with and approved by the NYSDEC 
and the USFWS.  The approved Monitoring Plan and the identification of all equipment 
(e.g., gauges, markers, and/or other measuring devices) to determine head pond elevation, 
bypass flow, and rate of impoundment elevation change will be filed with the 
Commission within 6 months of the issuance and acceptance of the new license, or the 
Effective Date of the new license, whichever is later.  The Monitoring Plan and the 
associated equipment will provide a means of independent verification by the NYSDEC 
and the USFWS of the Project’s minimum bypass flow.  The Licensee shall ensure that 
all monitoring equipment required by Monitoring Plan, including head pond and/or tail 
water gauges, shall be made operational and calibrated within 18 months of license 
issuance.  
3.4.2 Record Keeping 
As to be defined by the Stream Flow and Water Level Monitoring Plan, the 
Licensee shall keep accurate and sufficient records of the impoundment elevations, 
bypass flows, and the rate of impoundment elevation change. Such data shall be 
maintained in spreadsheet format in intervals ranging from 15 minutes to 1 hour, and in 
increments ranging from 0.1 foot to 1.0 foot.  A copy of the Monitoring Plan and all 
associated records will be made available for visual inspection at the Licensee’s Hydro 
Page 69 of 71
Exhibit __ (CCE-31) - Part D 


--- Page 1275 ---
Project No. 2934-029 
 
- 70 - 
 
 
 
Site within 5 business days of a request from the NYSDEC, or provided to the NYSDEC 
in written form within 30 days of the Licensee’s receipt of a written request for such 
records by the NYSDEC.  In support of implementing the Monitoring Plan, the NYSDEC 
will provide the Licensee with a contact person to receive such information.  In addition, 
the Licensee will provide to the NYSDEC the name of a 7 day-per-week contact person 
or persons to provide timely verification of monitored flows, rate of impoundment 
elevation change, and responses to questions regarding abnormal or emergency 
conditions. 
3.4.3 Justification 
The Parties believe that the development of a Stream Flow and Water Level 
Monitoring Plan and the associated measurement and data management activities are an 
essential component of a water flow and elevation management program.  Such a 
Monitoring Plan, and the associated implementation of the Plan, provides the tools 
necessary to verify the water flows and elevations agreed to in this Offer of Settlement, 
and provides a systematic means of tracking flow and elevation compliance.  Aside from 
providing the agencies a means to independently monitor bypass flows, the visual 
gauge(s) or marker(s) will be useful to the Licensee as well. 
The purpose of the Monitoring Plan is to allow the NYSDEC and the USFWS an 
independent means to determine how closely the Project complies with required 
operations.  While the Licensee will be allowed to fluctuate the impoundment as directed 
by the NYSCC in support of navigation and canal operations, the Parties believe that the 
ability to monitor the required bypass flow and rate of impoundment elevation change is 
essential to the Project’s compliance program.  Through the establishment of a means 
(gauge[s] and/or marker[s]) to verify the Project’s bypass flow, as well as record keeping 
to verify the rate of impoundment elevation change, the Parties will have a sufficient 
means of confirming the Project’s compliance with the agreed-to operational measures. 
3.5 
Threatened and Endangered Species 
3.5.1 General Agreements 
The Licensee has consulted with the USFWS and the NYSDEC and has identified 
the northern long-eared bat and bald eagle as species of concern that could be found 
within the Project area.  In order to address the management of these species relative to 
Project operations, the Licensee has developed a Northern Long-Eared Bat Management 
Plan and Bald Eagle Management Plan in consultation with, and with the approval of, the 
NYSDEC and the USFWS.  Copies of the approved plans are presented in Attachments 
A and B, respectively, to this Offer of Settlement.  The plans include measures to provide 
Page 70 of 71
Exhibit __ (CCE-31) - Part D 


--- Page 1276 ---
Project No. 2934-029 
 
- 71 - 
 
 
 
protection to both northern long-eared bats and bald eagles.  Upon issuance of the new 
license by the Commission, the Licensee will implement the Northern Long-Eared Bat 
Management and Bald Eagle Management Plans. 
3.5.2 Justification 
The northern long-eared bat is protected under the Endangered Species Act and 
the bald eagle is protected under the Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act and the 
Migratory Bird Treaty Act.  Additionally, both species are protected by the State of New 
York.  Removal of trees could potentially affect northern long-eared bats and bald eagles.  
The Parties agree that implementation of the Northern Long-Eared Bat and Bald Eagle 
Management Plans, presented in Attachments A and B, respectively, to this Offer of 
Settlement will minimize future Project-related impacts that may affect these species. 
 
3.6 
Invasive Species 
3.6.1 General Agreements 
Upon the issuance and acceptance of the new license, or the Effective Date of the 
new license, whichever is later, the Licensee will implement the Invasive Species 
Management Plan that has been developed in consultation with the NYSDEC and the 
USFWS.  A copy of the approved plan is presented in Attachment D to this Offer of 
Settlement.  The plan includes measures to prevent or limit the introduction and/or spread 
of invasive species during construction, maintenance, and operational activities 
associated with the Project, as defined by the NYSDEC Office of Invasive Species 
Coordination. 
3.6.2 Justification 
Although no invasive species were identified within the Project boundary during 
the relicensing studies, the Parties agree that implementation of the Invasive Species 
Management Plan presented in Attachment D to this Offer of Settlement will be 
beneficial to help prevent the introduction of invasive species to the Project through 
consultation activities or hydropower operations.

letter is to provide the Commission with a progress and schedule update relating to this effort. 
As discussed in the March 29, 2019 letter to the Commission, NYSEG is performing an evaluation of 
the left abutment area, including a dye study to develop a long-term solution to address the condition 
of the left abutment concrete and the stone masonry wall at the upstream abutment face. By letter 
dated September 12, 2019, the Commission approved the Drilling Plan and Proposed Dye Study at 
the left abutment of the Kent Falls Development. NYSEG has coordinated with the New York State 
Department of Environmental Conservation (NYSDEC) regarding the use of environmentally 
friendly/biodegradable dyes to support the dye study. Consultation with the NYSDEC is attached to 
this letter.  
The wells for the dye study were installed in October 2019, however, due to river conditions and 
associated access challenges, NYSEG has been unable to install the proposed collection system to 
support the dye study. In lieu of the collection system, staff from Atlantic Testing Laboratories (ATL) 
made visual observations of discharges from the weep holes and downstream areas following injection 
of the dye. The logs of the visual observations are attached to this letter.  No visible dye was observed 
at the weeps during the study period. NYSEG will continue to work with the engineering consultant to 
complete the design of improvements to address the condition of the structure in accordance with the 
plan and schedule below.

NYSEG Kents Falls Left Abutment Project Update 
Dear Mr. Spain: 
By letter dated October 19, 2017 from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC or 
Commission), following a September 20, 2017 FERC annual dam safety inspection, New York State 
Electric and Gas (NYSEG) was requested to provide a plan and schedule to repair the erosion/void 
(about 2’ diameter) observed along the water line at the upstream spillway concrete left abutment of 
the NYSEG Kent Falls Dam. By letter dated March 29, 2019, NYSEG provided an updated plan and 
schedule to the FERC to perform engineering design, project planning and initiate construction 
procurement in 2019 and to execute repair work in 2020. Following a dye study performed in 2019 
and 2020, NYSEG provided an updated plan and schedule on December 22, 2020. The engineering 
and detailed design for the left abutment repairs was completed in 2021; attached, the Commission 
will find the compressed drawing set for these repairs. The purpose of this letter is to provide the 
Commission with a progress and schedule update relating to this effort. 
Below is an updated plan and schedule to address the left abutment condition.

Engineering and Detailed Design Completion: 2021 (completed)
•
Procurement of Construction Contractor: 2022-2023
•
Construction: 2024

ES-1
I. 
Executive Summary
New York State Electric & Gas Corporation (NYSEG) and Rochester Gas and Electric Corporation
(RG&E) (collectively, the “Companies”) have been pursuing resiliency improvements in our
transmission and distribution systems to reduce the frequency and impact of outages from severe
weather and major storms. We recognize that improving grid resiliency is critical for maintaining safe,
reliable electricity service for our customers and communities in response to growing risks from climate
change. The Companies have been working to modernize our grids while incorporating changes to our
planning, engineering, and maintenance programs to reduce the impacts of major storms on our
customers.
Priorities for
the next three
years
Create connections between Resiliency Plan circuits and adjacent circuits that will
provide a backup power source when power outages occur (“circuit ties”) and use
automation technology to allow NYSEG and RG&E to operate these circuit ties
without the need to send electrical workers into the field (“automation”).
Utilize Avangrid’s Distribution Resiliency Guide to apply stronger designs and
infrastructure standards to the Resiliency Plan circuits so that the circuit ties can
reduce the frequency and impact of outages (“hardening”).
Apply Enhanced Vegetation Management (“EVM”) techniques as appropriate to
reduce the probability of tree-caused outages along targeted line sections.
Demonstrate how our Resiliency Programs can decrease the frequency and impact
of outages for our customers in response to increasing climate risks.
Implementing the Resiliency Plan will significantly reduce the frequency and duration of outages on 65
circuits during severe weather conditions and major storms. These circuits have been selected based
on an analysis of outages over the 2019-2021 period, including major storms. NYSEG and RG&E have
developed a solution for each circuit that achieves optimal results to achieve the two objectives of
resiliency: (1) reducing damage from major storms and (2) minimizing the number of customer hours
without power. NYSEG is requesting approval for approximately $152 million over four years (2023 to
2026) to complete the improvements as part of the Resiliency Plan. RG&E is requesting approval for
approximately $55 over four years. Tables ES-1 and ES-2 identify the circuits, resiliency programs, and
costs for projects with detailed scoping complete.

Benefit-Cost Analysis
The Companies retained Resource Innovations to complete a benefit-cost analysis (BCA) that
compares the costs of the improvements recommended in the Resiliency Plan to the benefits the
improvements will produce. Detailed results of the BCA and a full explanation of the methodology are
included in Appendix C.
The BCA is applied on a forward-looking basis to investments that typically have significant upfront
costs but have benefits that accrue over multiple years. The analysis was developed according to the
Joint Utilities of New York BCA Handbook.3 It focuses primarily on the societal test, which accounts for
the benefits customers receive from avoiding power interruptions and the operational benefits that a
utility receives. Results for the Utility Cost Test (UCT) and Ratepayer Impact Measure (RIM) are also
included.
The combined Resiliency Investments for NYSEG and RG&E have a positive net present value (NPV)
of $59.8 million and a benefit/cost ratio of 1.5 over 30 years. NPV refers to the net value of all future
cost and benefit streams over the life of an investment, discounted to the present.
The benefit/cost ratios for the UCT and RIM tests are much lower than those for the societal test. This
is because the UCT and RIM methodologies exclude the avoided interruptions costs that accrue to
customers from the resiliency improvements.
Figure ES-1 and Table ES-3 summarize the BCA results4.

1 Introduction
This Resiliency Plan is a critical part of our long-term strategy to strengthen our grid. It extends learning
from recent resiliency projects to a greater portion of NYSEG and RG&E’s distribution systems. The
NYSEG/RG&E plan targets 65 circuits that have experienced severe outage impacts from extreme
weather and where we can make a dramatic improvement in the quality of service that our customers
experience. Implementing this plan will help us gain experience and refine our resiliency programs to
deliver the best results economically.
This Report
Presents the Companies’ requests for incremental funding for resiliency
improvements.
Explains how resiliency improvements will reduce the impact of severe weather on
electricity service for our customers.
Explains the difference between reliability and resiliency in the Companies’
approach to addressing power interruptions due to severe weather.
Describes the Companies’ Resiliency Programs, and how they are being applied to
the circuits involved in the Resiliency Plan.
Summarizes the Resiliency Projects included in the Resiliency Plan.
Presents the benefits of the Resiliency Plan improvements, including a summary of
a Benefit-Cost Analysis.
This report uses terms that are related but distinct. The following definitions are intended to help the
reader with the distinctions.
Resiliency: (1) Preventing and limiting the scope and impact of outages when they occur, and (2)
the ability to expediently restore power after a significant outage. Resiliency is discussed in more
detail in Section 2.
Resiliency Program: An established approach for improving resiliency. Programs may include
traditional or new system designs, technologies, and maintenance techniques or combinations.
Resiliency Project: A specific recommendation to improve the resiliency of a portion of the
Companies’ transmission and distribution systems. A resiliency project includes a description of the
improvement need, technical details of the recommended solution, a solution deployment schedule,
and a cost estimate.
Resiliency Plan: A Resiliency Plan is a collection of Resiliency Projects to be implemented during
a specified period.
The following sections provide background on how the Companies are working to address the impacts
of major storms on the electric service that we provide our customers. We highlight crucial differences
between resiliency and reliability, and how targeted resiliency programs can reduce the frequency and
duration of the outages that our New York customers have experienced because of the most severe
weather events. The Resiliency Plan identifies specific improvements on 31 of our hardest-hit circuits
and explains how these improvements can dramatically improve service quality for customers.

2 Reliability and Resiliency
2.1 Vulnerability to Climate Risks
The resiliency of energy supply and delivery has long been an objective of regulation, along with
affordability, reliability, and safety. Resiliency has recently become the focus following major storms
that cause extended outages on electrical transmission and distribution (T&D) systems or a spike in
energy costs from a disruption in fuel supply. The industry and policy responses to these disruptions
are generally reactive and include calls for investigations, audits, or other actions that can lead to
improvements.
However, the frequency and severity of storms and evidence of climate change have reached a level of
concern that requires a proactive response to address the risks to utility infrastructure tailored to New
York’s circumstances. These include the primary climate risks facing New York, the ability of the
existing infrastructure to withstand these climate risks given the New York topography, and the threat
from both factors on service to customers and public safety more broadly.
Our service areas are particularly vulnerable to intense windstorms, heavy thunderstorms with lightning
and substantial precipitation, occasional tornadic activity, ice storms, and heavy snowstorms that can
cause widespread damage to the overhead T&D system. Portions of the Companies’ T&D facilities may
also be susceptible to flooding due to sea-level rise in the future.
Moreover, parts of the Companies’ systems are characterized by extraordinarily long distribution
circuits serving heavily wooded rural areas. This combination exposes the existing infrastructure to
storms that cause large branches and entire trees to fall and lengthens outages for customers that lose
power.
The key risks to the Companies and their customers from climate change include:
 
Infrastructure damage from more frequent and intense storms accompanied by heavy snow, ice,
and high winds;
 
Increased demand for electricity – along with decreased transmission capacity and efficiency -
during the summer peak hours due to higher temperatures; and
 
Customer health, safety, and comfort impacts from power outages lasting multiple days.
There are several actions that NYSEG and RG&E can take to enhance resiliency. They include:
 
More aggressive vegetation management, including hazard tree removal;
 
Application of animal guards to prevent rodents and other creatures from contacting energized
wires and equipment;
 
Establishment of more robust design standards for poles and other utility infrastructure
(“hardening”); and
 
Distribution automation and topology changes that enable circuit reconfiguration and power
rerouting.
More innovative solutions for enhancing resiliency include distributed generation, energy storage, and
microgrids.

2.2 Reliability Versus Resiliency
“Reliability” refers to the ability of an electric distribution utility to deliver the desired quantity of quality
power to all customers when needed. Reliability is typically measured and reported for a specified
period using a set of widely accepted industry metrics. NYSEG and RG&E measure reliability using
standard metrics as defined by the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) and calculate
these metrics by including and excluding “Major Event Days,” also referred to as “Major Storms.”5
Resiliency, or resilience, is different from reliability. The Companies define “resiliency” as (1) preventing
and limiting the scope and impact of outages when they occur and (2) the ability to expediently restore
power after a significant outage. Thus, resiliency is both the ability of a system to withstand forces that
could potentially cause damage and the ability to limit the impact of events and restore service when
damage occurs. Resiliency pertains to all outages, including major storms.
Factors that contribute to the desire to address resiliency include:
 
Longer restoration time;
 
Geographically widespread outages6;
 
Extensive damage to infrastructure;
 
Importance of coordination with public agencies and first responders; and

Need for mutual assistance resources such as outside utility crews.
The distinction between resiliency and reliability is particularly relevant when developing a plan that
addresses both objectives.

The Companies employ several programs to maintain the safety and reliability of the distribution
system. These programs have been developed and refined over many years to deliver high reliability at
an affordable cost for our customers. Reliability programs are focused on identifying, correcting, and
preventing conditions that could lead to power interruptions during blue or gray sky days.7
In response to severe weather and major storms, NYSEG, RG&E, and the other Avangrid operating
companies have been developing new approaches to help prevent the outages that would typically
occur under these conditions. However, we recognize that hardening our infrastructure to avoid all
outages is not possible at a cost that our customers would want to pay. Therefore, we also want to use
Resiliency Programs that leverage new technologies and operational techniques to provide backup
power sources and restore customers more quickly when outages inevitably occur during the worst
weather.

Innovative Solutions
Resiliency and reliability are also related in meaningful ways, mainly when focusing on a particular
circuit. Planning of reliability and resiliency programs should be coordinated with standard and
enhanced vegetation management as the most obvious example. Tracking investments and expenses
must be performed to avoid any double counting for ratemaking purposes. This can be accomplished
by ensuring that resiliency investments and costs are incremental. Finally, performance measurement
should be done both with and without major storms. Both outcomes provide insights that are helpful
when designing reliability and resiliency solutions, particularly when examined over a multi-year period.
2.3 Outage Impacts from Storms
From 2019 through 2021, the Companies recorded approximately 62,000 interruption events. Those
outages affected almost seven million customers for more than 24 million customer outage hours over
three years. The Companies classify interruption events as Storm or non-Storm.8 Over the course of a
typical year, the number of non-Storm events is more than two times the number of Storm events for
NYSEG, and more than six times for RG&E. However, Storm events cause the most damage, requiring
more time for restoration, and resulting in more customer outage hours (Figure 2).
7  The reliability programs are described in more detail in Appendix B.
8  NYSEG and RGE classify each interruption event as “storm” or “non-storm”. While all “major storm” events would be classified as “storms”,
not all “storm” interruptions are part of “major storms.”

Major storms can affect large portions of our service territories and cause outages that take many days

major storms and their impacts for NYSEG and RG&E. The Resiliency Plan targets improvements to
reduce the damage from these events, but also to reduce the amount of time needed to restore power
to our customers. These improvements will also reduce customer outage hours during non-storm
events.

3 Resiliency Programs
The Companies’ Resiliency Programs are designed to be applied as a supplement to existing reliability
programs and target resiliency more directly. Their primary purpose is to (1) prevent and limit the scope
and impact of outages and (2) increase our ability to restore power after a significant outage quickly,
consistent with the Companies’ definition of resiliency.
As shown in Table 4, NYSEG and RG&E have four Resiliency Programs designed to strengthen our
systems and make them more resistant to damage and related outages.

This Resiliency Plan focuses on two of these programs, with application of a third program as
appropriate. None of the projects proposed for these Resiliency Plans include improvements classified
as “innovative solutions.” However, Distribution Planning considers innovative solutions including
distributed energy resources and other advanced technologies as part of the Comprehensive Area
Study process.
3.1 Infrastructure Hardening
Infrastructure hardening is a critical part of improving system resiliency. These programs target
infrastructure susceptible to tree contact and damage during severe weather. Infrastructure hardening
is the focus of Avangrid’s Distribution Resiliency Guide.

3.1.1 Stronger, contact-resistant conductor
The Companies’ overhead distribution systems have been built over decades, with multiple sizes and
designs of conductors. Most of these overhead conductors are bare (uninsulated). Some are smaller
than Avangrid’s current standards or made of material that is less resistant to physical damage or
breakage from tree contact. For new construction, Avangrid’s Distribution Resiliency Guide specifies
that bare aluminum wire will be used in areas where tree encroachment is not possible. Tree wire will
be used in areas where tree encroachment is likely.9 Tree wire is an aluminum conductor covered with
multiple layers of material that provides electrical insulation and physical protection from incidental tree
contact. Tree wire has been shown to reduce electrical faults from tree contact dramatically. When
used in spacer cable configurations, overhead distribution lines can withstand impacts from larger
branches.
3.1.2 Replacement of failure-prone poles
Experience has shown that stronger poles are significantly less prone to failure from storm damage.
Avangrid’s Distribution Resiliency Guide specifies that only Class 1, 2, or 3 poles will be used for new
construction.10 The purpose of this specification is to improve the resiliency of distribution systems
during storms and severe weather. This Resiliency Plan calls for replacing poles on Plan circuits that
have been identified as defective as part of the DLI program. These poles are proposed for
replacement as part of circuit resiliency plans and are in addition to those that will be replaced as part
of the standard DLI program.
3.1.3 Selective undergrounding
Undergrounding is the replacement of overhead primary electric wires with underground cables. From a
resiliency perspective, undergrounding makes the power lines less susceptible to outages during high
winds, thunderstorms, heavy snow, or ice storms. Some communities and municipalities express an
9  Tree encroachment is defined as where there is a reasonable possibility that trees and or branches can potentially be in contact with
energized primary overhead wires. See “Avangrid Distribution Resiliency Guide Up to 35 kV,” Revision 0, 2019, Section 5 – Distribution
Primary OH Wires – Up To 35 kV.
10 Ibid. Section 4 – Available Distribution Wood Poles.

interest in undergrounding because of the aesthetic benefits and the resiliency benefits it can provide.
However, undergrounding of wire and associated infrastructure is usually uneconomic except in
densely populated areas. Undergrounding may be a viable option where common facilities support
multiple overhead circuits, such as at substation gateways in urban communities.
3.1.4 Design standards for increased resiliency
In 2019 Avangrid introduced the Distribution Resiliency Guide for infrastructure operating at voltages up
to 35 kV. The Distribution Resiliency Guide was developed in response to severe storms experienced
by Avangrid and its customers in the northeast. The Companies are using the Distribution Resiliency
Guide to improve the ability of their distribution systems to better withstand the impacts of storms. The
plans presented in this report incorporate design standards from the Distribution Resiliency Guide.
Going forward, NYSEG and RG&E plan to use the Guide to increase system resiliency in parts of the
system where it is needed.
3.2 Topology with Automation
A distribution system topology describes the configuration of infrastructure that comprises the
distribution system. Most of the distribution systems of NYSEG and RG&E consist of radial circuits.
These circuits are characterized by a design in which power is received at a substation from the
transmission system and distributed to customers via three-phase or single-phase lines. In NYSEG’s
service territory, long circuits often serve multiple communities and are exposed to many miles of trees
along their rights-of-way. An interruption caused by a single tree can affect numerous homes,
businesses, and public safety infrastructure, creating a critical resiliency challenge. This circumstance
is exacerbated during major storms when there are multiple damage sites along a circuit.
3.2.1 Circuit Ties
The Resiliency Plans propose adding circuit ties for most projects. A circuit tie creates an alternate
power source by connecting to an adjacent circuit served by a different substation. If the power from the
primary source is lost due to an upstream outage, the circuit tie can be closed to route power from the
alternate source. Adding automated switching makes it possible to quickly transfer customers from the
primary source to the alternate source so that the interruption they experience is short. These
automated reclosers and SCADA switches are described below. Figure 7 illustrates a generic circuit tie
project.

3.2.2 Distribution reclosers and SCADA switches
Reclosers and switches are electrical devices that allow utilities to connect and disconnect portions of a
distribution circuit to an upstream power source. Strategically placed reclosers and switches can help
isolate faulted parts of a distribution feeder and reduce the number of customers that lose power when
a fault occurs. The Companies can automate reclosers and switches to enable remote or coordinated
control by sophisticated automatic switching schemes. Fault Location, Isolation, and Service
Restoration (FLISR) is an available distribution automation application that uses reclosers and switches
to automatically reconfigure one or more distribution circuits to isolate faulted portions of a distribution
feeder and keep power flowing to as many customers as possible.
The Resiliency Plan includes the accelerated deployment of devices that enable switching automation
functions on circuits: distribution reclosers and SCADA switches. Over time, NYSEG and RG&E will
increase the capabilities and benefits11 of these devices by integrating their operation with distribution
management systems (DMS). The DMS is part of a broader grid modernization strategy and Platform
Technology roadmap.
Distribution Reclosers
Reclosers have relays that can detect the excessive electric current associated with a short circuit
(fault) caused by a tree contact, animal contact, or other abnormal condition. Upon detection of a fault,
the recloser can open to safely interrupt the fault current and de-energize the downstream portion of the
11  These future benefits are not captured in the Benefit-Cost Analysis for this Resiliency Plan.
Exhibit __ (CCE-44)
Page 16 of 45


--- Page 1319 ---
NYSEG | RG&E | 2023-2026 Resiliency Plan
11
circuit until crews can fix the problem. Some faults, such as a tree branch brushing against a line, can
be temporary and not require repair. Reclosers can be programmed to reconnect (“reclose”) the
downstream circuit quickly. If the fault is cleared, the recloser remains closed and downstream
customers may only lose power for a moment. If the fault is not cleared, the recloser may “reclose”
multiple times (typically up to three times) and “lockout.” The utility must send a crew to remove the
fault, repair any damage, and reconnect the line safely.
SCADA switches
SCADA switches have telecommunications and intelligence that enable remote and coordinated
operation without an onsite crew. These automated switches are often used with reclosers and help
operators isolate an outage and connect customers to an alternate power source. Unlike reclosers,
utilities do not use these switches to interrupt faults. However, fault detection capability built into these
switches can help utility operators identify and locate the source of a fault more quickly.
3.2.3 Line upgrades, voltage conversions, and step-transformers
Creating a circuit tie requires sufficient capacity and voltage support on both circuits so that each one
can serve additional customers during restoration. Sometimes this requires upgrading portions of each
circuit to 3-phase and replacing conductors with a larger size. Adding voltage support with a voltage
regulator or capacitor bank might also be needed. In some cases, the Companies may want to connect
two circuits that operate at different voltages, for example, one at 12.47 kV and the other at 34.5 kV. In
such a case, a step-transformer is needed. Engineers and planners might also consider adding a new
circuit. However, no new circuits are proposed in the 2023-2026 Resiliency Plans.
3.2.4 Substation upgrades
Upgraded and new substations, along with sub-transmission lines and circuit breakers, enable NYSEG
and RG&E to create new circuits reducing the outage exposure to customers located on long circuits.
They may also provide a second transmission feed into a substation to protect against the loss of a sole
power source.
3.3 Enhanced Vegetation Management
The Companies’ standard vegetation management reliability programs work to maintain clearance
between vegetation and distribution system infrastructure on over 34,000 miles of distribution lines. The
programs have two main parts:
1. Inspecting and pruning all forested rights-of-way every five years12 to standard clearances as
shown in Figure 4. This “cycle” trimming program also includes tree removal inside rights-of-way.
2. Supplemental “hot-spot” pruning for faster-growing vegetation species that could encroach upon
electric facilities before subsequent cycle trimming occurs (i.e., within the five-year cycle).
12  Trimming on a five-year cycle has been considered an industry standard and utility good practice. NYSEG is proposing the adoption of five-
year cycle trimming as part of the 2022 rate case.

For the circuits included in the Resiliency Plans, the Companies may apply enhanced “ground-to-sky”
clearance (i.e., “Enhanced Vegetation Management” or EVM) as appropriate in conjunction with the
Topology with Automation and Hardening resiliency programs. In developing the circuit plans,
engineers and field technicians worked hard to coordinate and optimize multiple improvements to
deliver best-value resiliency to customers. The Companies intend to update the Resiliency Plans with
targeted EVM as resiliency circuits are identified in future years.
3.4 Innovative Solutions
The Companies’ Resiliency Plans applies modern grid technologies for automation and topology
improvements that make it possible to provide alternate power sources when outages occur. NYSEG
and RG&E are also looking at ways to apply emerging non-wires solutions in places where
conventional wired infrastructure may be impractical or prohibitively expensive. This includes distributed
generation, energy storage, and microgrids that support continuity of service for customers and
communities during major events. The Java Microgrid project described below is an example of an
innovative solution for improving resiliency. Distribution Planning evaluates these types of solutions as
part of the Comprehensive Area Study process.
Java Microgrid Project
Java substation is a 34.5/4.8 kV substation serving approximately 1,700 customers in NYSEG’s
Lancaster Division. The substation is fed from a 34.5 kV transmission line and feeds two distribution
circuits from a single station transformer. As part of a needs assessment, NYSEG’s planning engineers
evaluated options for providing a backup power source for the Java substation following the loss of the
substation transformer or the 34.5 kV transmission line.
The proposed solution is a microgrid utilizing a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) as the backup
power source for the substation and distribution feeders. The microgrid can isolate from the 34.5 kV
system during an outage event and serve customers for up to 8 hours under most conditions using the

energy stored in the BESS. NYSEG’s grid operators will be able to monitor and coordinate
BESS/microgrid operation with other distribution devices.
3.5 Proven Results
Avangrid has gained valuable experience with recent resiliency projects in our New York and Maine
service areas. These projects demonstrate the efficacy of resiliency programs and improved resiliency
as measured by the number of customers affected by interruptions and the number of customer outage
hours.
3.5.1 NYSEG Resiliency Improvements
NYSEG completed targeted resiliency projects over the past two years. Comparing data from before
and after the completion of the resiliency improvements, NYSEG saw a 25% reduction in the number of
customers affected by interruptions.
3.5.2 Central Maine Power Resiliency Project
In 2021, NYSEG’s affiliate, Central Maine Power (CMP), completed two projects to increase customer
resiliency and service reliability in the Alfred and Skowhegan/Jackman areas. These projects included
overhead circuit hardening with tree-wire and spacer cable, changes to circuit topology in the form of a
circuit tie and supporting capacitor bank, and distribution automation to enable sectionalizing. CMP saw
a 29% reduction in the number of customers affected by interruptions following the resiliency
improvements. The improvement was 49% for tree-caused outages.

4 The 2023-2026 Resiliency Plan
4.1 Developing the Resiliency Projects
The projects included in the Resiliency Plan were identified and defined by applying a three-stage
process (Figure 5) with involvement from multiple teams from across NYSEG and RG&E. Our goal was
to identify distribution circuits that would most benefit from the kinds of improvements that the
Companies’ resiliency programs can deliver. The ultimate goal is to improve service quality for our
customers while minimizing cost increases and accounting for engineering, permitting procurement,
and construction constraints.
Figure 5. Developing the list of Resiliency Projects.
4.1.1 Stage 1 – Identify Worst Performing Resiliency Circuits
Targeting our worst-performing resiliency circuits helps the Companies ensure that our resiliency
investments will deliver the greatest “bang for the buck” for our customers. As explained in Section 2,
NYSEG and RG&E have long used IEEE Standard 1366 and its industry-standard reliability metrics to
track reliability performance over time. For the Resiliency Plan, the Companies used a tailored metric,
Weighted-SAIFI, designed to identify circuits that would most benefit from the targeted application of
our resiliency programs. Weighted-SAIFI is determined in three steps:
1. Calculate the SAIFI for each circuit, including outages from storms, over the past calendar year.
Including outages from storms helps ensure we account for severe weather conditions that our
resiliency programs address.
2. Calculate the SAIFI contribution of each circuit to the total system SAIFI.
3. Multiply the SAIFI of each circuit by its SAIFI contribution. This creates the Weighted-SAIFI metric.
The weather has a significant impact on SAIFI. The year-to-year variability can be substantial when
including MEDs and looking at SAIFI at the circuit level. To account for this, NYSEG and RG&E looked
at the average Weighted-SAIFI for each circuit over three years, from 2019 to 2021. We ranked all
circuits according to the three-year average Weighted-SAIFI, with number 1 having the highest value.
We took the quartile with the highest Weighted-SAIFI scores to Stage 2.
Exhibit __ (CCE-44)
Page 20 of 45


--- Page 1323 ---
NYSEG | RG&E | 2023-2026 Resiliency Plan
15
4.1.2 Stage 2 – Develop circuit improvement plans
Having identified the worst performing circuits, NYSEG and RG&E conducted detailed analyses of each
circuit to determine how to improve reliability and resiliency. Each plan incorporates input from
Comprehensive Area Studies, targeted engineering analysis at the circuit-level, and operational
information from our engineers and planners in the field. This information is analyzed to evaluate
options for ensuring that each circuit meets the Companies’ distribution planning criteria. The
improvement plans represent least-cost, best-fit solutions that consider each circuit’s performance
during severe weather, how outages can be avoided, and how service can be restored to customers
more quickly when outages happen.
Each project plan includes information such as:
 
Project location (substation and circuit);
 
Detailed project description, including electrical diagrams and construction steps;
 
Project needs/justification and benefits;
 
Solution alternatives and rationale for the recommended solution;
 
Funding details (improvement types and timing);
 
Start date and in-service date; and
 
Potential implementation constraints.
4.1.3 Stage 3 – Choose Resiliency Projects
In selecting the Resiliency Projects for this plan, NYSEG and RG&E focused on opportunities with three
key attributes.
First, identify projects that will make a difference and are cost-effective. Solutions should significantly
reduce storm-related power interruptions and the number of outage hours experienced by customers.
An expensive solution, such as a new substation, is not always affordable. Our teams try to develop
solutions that balance impact and affordability.
Second, coordinate resiliency solutions with other NYSEG and RG&E reliability programs such as DLI,
vegetation management, and distribution automation.
Third, assemble a portfolio of projects that meet capital budget targets and distribution planning
criteria.
4.2 Resiliency Project Summary
Implementing the Resiliency Plans will significantly reduce the frequency and duration of outages on
the targeted circuits during severe weather conditions and major storms. These circuits have been
selected based on an analysis of outages over the 2019-2021 period, including major storms. NYSEG
and RG&E have developed solutions for each circuit to achieve the two objectives of resiliency: (1)
reducing damage from major storms, and (2) minimizing the number of customer-hours without power.

timelines for the Companies’ Resiliency Plans for 2023-2026. NYSEG is requesting approval for $152

5 Summary of the Benefit-Cost Analyses (BCAs)
5.1 Overview
The Resiliency Plan represents incremental upfront investments that improve the Companies’ ability to
deliver distribution service by focusing directly on an attribute (resiliency) that is increasing in
importance to our customers and the communities we serve. A benefit-cost analysis (BCA) is a forward-
looking analysis that typically compares the costs of an up-front investment with the NPV of benefits
that accrue over multiple years. Regulators are often interested in a BCA when evaluating the costs of
a new program (e.g., an energy efficiency program or portfolio of programs), or a significant investment
that provides new functionality (e.g., a Smart Grid proposal).
The Companies retained Resource Innovations to perform a BCA of the 2023-2026 Resiliency Plan.
Resource Innovations’ BCA report15 presents a detailed description of their BCA methodology.
5.2 Methodology
The Resiliency Programs reduce the likelihood that severe weather will cause a power interruption for
our customers. The BCA includes assumptions about how each resiliency improvement will benefit
customers and the utility, either by reducing outages or reducing restoration and repair costs. Resource
Innovations has adopted a “societal” perspective when accounting for benefits. The societal test
evaluates whether the benefits, including externalities, exceed the costs. Thus, it not only counts
operational benefits to a utility, but it also includes benefits experienced by customers, such as reduced
outage costs.
Table 14 describes the costs and benefits of the Resiliency Programs in the BCA.

automation and hardening projects are capitalized. The incremental capital and O&M costs for each of
the eight circuits are presented in Section 4 as part of the description of each circuit improvement plan.
