35
All investments and avoided costs are all escalated at a rate of 2 percent per year. Future cost and
benefit streams are discounted at a rate of 7.87 percent per year for RG&E, and 7.49 percent per year
for NYSEG. The discount rates, which are used to calculate the present value of costs and benefits
over the life of the investments, are equal to the Companies’ after tax weighted average costs of capital
(WACC).16
Quantifying the impact of investments for a BCA involves first defining a base case, which represents a
projection of the future in the absence of the investment. Benefits are measured as the difference
between the future state with the investment and the base case. For this analysis, Resource
Innovations used a database of historical outages from 2019-2021 to represent the base case future
scenario. This period was selected because it covers multiple years and is recent enough that the
outages should reasonably reflect the performance of current grid infrastructure under current
conditions (i.e., the further back in time the baseline period stretches, the less reflective the outages will
be of current conditions). Resource Innovations worked with subject matter experts at Avangrid to
assess the impacts of the various resiliency measures on the existing database of outages to determine
how the investments would impact this baseline set of outages.
Particular care has been taken to avoid any double-counting of benefits among the resiliency programs.
For example. enhanced vegetation management reduces the frequency of tree-related outages, while
pole hardening reduces the frequency of pole-related outages. However, certain outages are classified
as both tree-related and pole-related. Similarly, the outages mitigated by automation and topology (A/T)
could also be tree-related or pole-related.
The largest source of benefits in the BCA is “avoided customer interruption costs.” When customers
experience interruptions, they bear economic costs. The Resiliency Plan investments are designed to
reduce the frequency and duration of interruptions and thus reduce the economic cost of those
interruptions to customers. The cost of customer interruptions was estimated using the Interruption
Cost Estimation (ICE) Model developed by Resource Innovations, in partnership with Lawrence
Berkeley National Laboratory, for the U.S. Department of Energy.17
The ICE Model uses historical NYSEG and RG&E outage and customer information to estimate the
cost of interruptions from the perspective of different customer classes, with and without the proposed
resiliency improvements. The model incorporates resiliency projects as they are implemented over
time, decreasing the frequency and duration of outages experienced by customers for multiple years
after the improvements are made. Model assumptions were adjusted to account for the severe weather
and storms that are the focus of the Resiliency Plans.
5.3 Results
The BCA calculates the net present value (NPV) of Resiliency Plan costs and benefits over a 30-year
analysis period. The costs of Resiliency Plan projects are modeled in the years they are incurred (2023
through 2026). Benefits begin in the year following each investment and repeat each year through the
end of useful life for equipment, or the end of the analysis period (2053), whichever comes first. All
16 The discount rate, which is used to calculate the present value of costs and benefits over the life of the investments, is the after tax weighted
average cost of capital (WACC) of each company.
17 https://icecalculator.com/documentation

36
costs and benefits are discounted to 2023 and a BCA ratio is calculated by dividing the NPV of benefits
by the NPV of costs.
Over 30 years, the Resiliency Plans for NYSEG and RG&E each produced positive NPVs and
benefit/cost ratios between 1.2 and 1.6 from a societal perspective.18 Most benefits come from avoided
interruption costs that accrue to customers. These results demonstrate the significant value that the
Companies’ Resiliency Plans can deliver for customers in the coming years. The benefit/cost ratios for
the UCT and RIM tests are much lower than those for the societal test. This is because the UCT and
RIM methodologies exclude the avoided interruptions costs that accrue to customers from the resiliency
improvements.

A-1
Appendix A: Classifying Events and Storms
Each type of day and storm characteristic presents unique challenges to the resilience of the electric
system. NYSEG and RG&E classify events as “major storms” when the number of affected customers
or the duration of customer outages meets threshold criteria.19 Weather that creates storm-classified
events includes:
 
Heavy snow/blizzard;
 
Heavy wet snow;
 
Lightning;
 
Heavy wind;
 
Rain;
 
Ice storm; and
 
Hurricane.
For years IEEE Standard 1366 has recommended tracking metrics such as SAIFI and SAIDI, including
or excluding MEDs. Excluding MEDs can help compare a utility’s reliability performance over time and
reliability performance among a cohort of utilities.  There is growing recognition that developing
resilience metrics requires looking at the system's performance over a broader range of conditions and
more severe events. Some industry organizations and experts have introduced terminology describing
the type of day associated with events of increasing severity. Table A-1 summarizes Blue Sky, Gray
Sky, and Black Sky days and how they can help describe events related to reliability and resiliency.
Table A-1. Types of days and their relationship to NYSEG/RG&E storm classifications.
Type of Day
Description
NYSEG/RG&E
Storm Classification

A day without a major storm or event that would cause
numerous customer interruptions.
None
No
Gray Sky Day
A day when a lower-severity storm or weather event might
cause significant customer interruptions.20
Minor
Maybe21
Black Sky Day
A day when a substantial portion of a utility’s customers
experience power interruptions due to a major storm or
other event that does severe damage to the grid.22

19 NYSEG and RG&E identify weather-related events as “major” when 10% or more of customers are affected, or if a customer experiences an
outage for more than 24 hours.
20  The non-storm resilience metric proposed by IEEE/DOE considers the number of gray sky days. See “Resilience Framework, Methods, and
Metrics for the Electricity Sector,” Technical Report PES-TR83, IEEE Power and Energy Society, October 2020.

depending on the outage data for all days during the reporting period (typically a year).
22  A black sky day is when more than 90% of a utility’s customers experience outages of more than 25 days. See “Resilience for Black Sky
Days,” Dr. Paul Stockton, for the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners, February 2014.

Appendix B: NYSEG and RG&E’s Reliability Programs
The following programs are part of the Companies’ “baseline” capital and O&M spending to support
reliability.
 
Distribution Line Inspection Program
 
Standard Vegetation Management Program
 
Substation Asset Management Program
 
Betterments Program
 
Smart Grid Program
5.3.1 Distribution Line Inspection (DLI) Program
The DLI program is a thorough, condition-based inspection of all distribution equipment on each
overhead structure. NYSEG and RG&E prioritize equipment repair and replacement by the criticality of
failure. Common issues include defective structural components such as crossarms and poles and
faulty equipment, including fused cutouts, line transformers, and insulators. Identifying weakened poles
is a critical part of the program. In addition to visual inspections, poles in service for more than 20 years
are sounded with a hammer to detect rot. The Companies coordinate the DLI and vegetation
management programs to improve operational efficiency and effectiveness. DLI inspections are
completed within a year of tree trimming and include a quality check to ensure that trimming meets
contractual specifications.
5.3.2 Standard Vegetation Management Program
Keeping trees away from distribution lines is critical for maintaining distribution system reliability and
resiliency in New York.23 The Companies’ vegetation management programs work to maintain
clearance between vegetation and distribution system infrastructure on over 34,000 miles of distribution
lines. The program has three parts:
3. Inspecting and pruning all forested rights-of-way every five years24 to standard clearances. This
“cycle” trimming program also includes the removal of trees inside rights-of-way.
4. Supplemental “hot-spot” pruning for faster-growing vegetation species that could encroach upon
electric facilities before subsequent cycle trimming occurs (i.e., within the five-year cycle).
5. Removal of selected “hazard” trees25 outside utility rights-of-way.
23  The US Department of Agriculture estimates that New York is 62.9% forested, the 10th most forested state in the US. See “Forest Inventory
and Analysis – Fiscal Year 2016 Business Report,” Table B-11, p. 71, United States Department of Agriculture, August 2017.
24  Trimming on a five-year cycle has been considered an industry standard and utility good practice.
25  Hazard trees are dead, declining, weak, uprooted, storm damaged, diseased trees, or tree species known to have a high failure rate that
are located such that there is a high probability of the tree contacting the electrical conductors if the tree were to fall. See “ANSI A300
Standards, Part 7 – Integrated Vegetation Management,” Tree Care Industry Association.

5.3.3 Substation Asset Management Program
Substations are critical components of the NYSEG and RG&E distribution systems as they provide the
source of power for distribution circuits. Substation equipment such as transformers, circuit breakers,
and structures has often been in reliable service for many years. The Companies monitor the condition
of this infrastructure to ensure ongoing reliability and identify equipment that has reached the end of
life. NYSEG and RG&E are investigating ways to prevent damage from flooding and other physical
threats related to climate change to improve the system’s resiliency.
5.3.4 Betterments Program
The Betterments program maintains the distribution system’s reliability, operability, and flexibility.
Distribution engineers evaluate circuits to identify deviations from reliability or distribution planning
criteria and coordinate with operations personnel to identify potential issues or concerns. These reviews
sometimes result in betterment project proposals. NYSEG and RG&E review and prioritize betterment
proposals to address potential reliability issues to prevent power interruptions.
5.3.5 Smart Grid Program
The Companies continue to implement their Smart Grid programs to improve the reliability and
efficiency of their systems. Deployment of platform technologies such as advanced metering
infrastructure (AMI), substation automation, distribution line automation, and advanced
telecommunications will help the Companies improve performance and meet the increasing
expectations of our customers. These technologies will also help integrate clean distributed energy
resources, electric vehicles, and other beneficial electrification applications.
